content.content:
=== framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force.md

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive force:
absolute strength (So) (the strength ceiling, confined in this text's own usage to maximum
involuntary strength, printed 107, which the text elsewhere says is not the same as a
measured isometric Fo, printed 147); starting-strength (SS) (the ability to develop the
greatest possible force at the very start of tension); acceleration-strength (AS) (the
ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun); and absolute
speed (Vo) (average velocity of an unloaded movement). Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. It is also stated that training
does not change this factor structure itself, only the relative importance and contribution
of each factor (printed 131). A discus-thrower factor-analysis example (Table 3.2, thigh
extension, PDF p. 152, printed p. 141) shows **absolute strength ranking first at every one
of the three torques tested** (24.0%, 32.1%, 34.7% as torque rises): starting strength drops
from 2nd (15.4%) to 4th (11.3%), while acceleration strength rises from 4th (12.2%) to 2nd
(16.2-17.2%) as torque rises. Absolute strength (So) is essentially uncorrelated with, or
mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the strength-speed
correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp. 140-144, 152,
printed pp. 129-133, 141, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve: they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio, printed as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978" (likely Viitasalo & Komi, verify).

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**;
the text does not say this is because AS and So are more genetically constrained, only that
they are "easier to perfect" (printed 133). **Inference:** this Ch3 material supplies a
quantified internal structure (four abilities, not just "RFD vs max force") that could
sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics are interpreted for a given athlete's load
profile; Eric's baseline lists modified RSI (mRSI) as the department's daily-readiness
marker and RFD/power among the "fluffy" ODSF metrics needing a specific rationale
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); this framework's four-component
breakdown is a candidate rationale, not a stated baseline position.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass)
should be judged mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive
back's first-step reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be
judged mainly on starting-strength and absolute speed markers. The same "explosiveness"
label hides two different training targets. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder, a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).
=== claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output.md

# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output

**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, the force developed
in knee extension or flexion is determined by hip joint angle, and maximal force in **hip
extension** in a seated position was found to occur at a 160° knee angle; but in a supine
leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a 100°-140° hip-angle
range (Lindeburg, 1964), a different measured quantity (knee-extension force, not
hip-extension force) under a different body position (supine versus seated). Knee-extension
strength increases 10-12%
when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
which changes the mechanical conditions of work, sometimes advantageously (full force
potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).

**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline** documents Olympic-lift-family
coaching (clean, snatch, jerk, squat) as core to Baylor's strength and power programming
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md
pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:** this claim gives a specific,
citable rationale for treating small positional cues within those lifts as directly
consequential, and for why a knee-extension test result at one angle or body position
should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or position, per the Lindeburg
finding above.

**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
verification.

# Strength Qualities and Muscle Groups Develop in a Fixed Order as Sports Mastery Grows, Not All at Once

**What it is** — The authors term "heterochronicity" the finding that, as sports mastery
grows, different strength qualities and different muscle groups develop their key role at
different times rather than simultaneously (Verkhoshansky's coinage for the phenomenon,

(So, confined in this text's own usage to maximum involuntary strength, see printed 107)

starting-strength (Ss) rises significantly only after that, tied to the introduction of
near-competition-intensity work (Fig 2.22a). (2) **Muscle-group order**: which muscle group
carries the "key" role for a skill shifts with mastery, e.g. in pole vaulting, the abdominal
muscles drive the initial pole-raising strength in novices, and the shoulder flexors take
over that functional role as mastery grows while elbow-extensor strength rises uniformly
over the same period (Nikonov & Verkhoshansky, Fig 2.21); in the shot put, the correlation
between athletic result and arm-muscle strength drops from 0.83 (novices) to 0.73 (elite),
while the correlation with leg strength rises from 0.37 (novices) to 0.87 (elite)
(Verkhoshansky & Purvin). A related sequence is given for starting-strength in jumpers and
sprinters: ankle flexion develops first (bearing the earliest, most intense load), then hip
extension (grouped with knee extension in the text's discussion), and finally hip flexion,
developing later and less intensely (hip flexors only oppose gravity and one limb's inertia,
a smaller demand). The text separately notes that the approximately linear rise of maximum
and absolute strength described above is typical only of sports where the athlete overcomes
relatively small resistance and the speed of producing force matters more than its
magnitude (printed 114); this caveat attaches to that linear-rise finding specifically, not
to the three-quality development order as a whole. (PDF pp. 123-126, printed pp. 112-115,
Figs 2.21-2.22.)

which quality receives the heaviest training emphasis at each stage: absolute strength work
dominates early training, speed-strength work is introduced next, and specialized,
near-competition-intensity work (which most directly trains starting-strength) comes latest
in a periodized plan. For the muscle-group order, they attribute it to which muscle groups
bear the largest mechanical load at each stage of skill development (e.g. ankle flexors are
loaded most intensely from the very start of ground-contact-based skills, hip flexors much
less so, since they only move a single limb against gravity).

then starting-strength) as a rough sequencing guide within a periodized plan, consistent with

already-strong athletes shifting more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work

=== framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force.md

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive force:
absolute strength (So) (the strength ceiling, confined in this text's own usage to maximum
involuntary strength, printed 107, which the text elsewhere says is not the same as a
measured isometric Fo, printed 147); starting-strength (SS) (the ability to develop the
greatest possible force at the very start of tension); acceleration-strength (AS) (the
ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun); and absolute
speed (Vo) (average velocity of an unloaded movement). Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. It is also stated that training
does not change this factor structure itself, only the relative importance and contribution
of each factor (printed 131). A discus-thrower factor-analysis example (Table 3.2, thigh
extension, PDF p. 152, printed p. 141) shows **absolute strength ranking first at every one
of the three torques tested** (24.0%, 32.1%, 34.7% as torque rises): starting strength drops
from 2nd (15.4%) to 4th (11.3%), while acceleration strength rises from 4th (12.2%) to 2nd
(16.2-17.2%) as torque rises. Absolute strength (So) is essentially uncorrelated with, or
mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the strength-speed
correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp. 140-144, 152,
printed pp. 129-133, 141, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve: they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio, printed as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978" (likely Viitasalo & Komi, verify).

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**;
the text does not say this is because AS and So are more genetically constrained, only that
they are "easier to perfect" (printed 133). **Inference:** this Ch3 material supplies a
quantified internal structure (four abilities, not just "RFD vs max force") that could
sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics are interpreted for a given athlete's load
profile; Eric's baseline lists modified RSI (mRSI) as the department's daily-readiness
marker and RFD/power among the "fluffy" ODSF metrics needing a specific rationale
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); this framework's four-component
breakdown is a candidate rationale, not a stated baseline position.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass)
should be judged mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive
back's first-step reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be
judged mainly on starting-strength and absolute speed markers. The same "explosiveness"
label hides two different training targets. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder, a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).
=== claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output.md

# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output

**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, the force developed
in knee extension or flexion is determined by hip joint angle, and maximal force in **hip
extension** in a seated position was found to occur at a 160° knee angle; but in a supine
leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a 100°-140° hip-angle
range (Lindeburg, 1964), a different measured quantity (knee-extension force, not
hip-extension force) under a different body position (supine versus seated). Knee-extension
strength increases 10-12%
when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
which changes the mechanical conditions of work, sometimes advantageously (full force
potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).

**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline** documents Olympic-lift-family
coaching (clean, snatch, jerk, squat) as core to Baylor's strength and power programming
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md
pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:** this claim gives a specific,
citable rationale for treating small positional cues within those lifts as directly
consequential, and for why a knee-extension test result at one angle or body position
should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or position, per the Lindeburg
finding above.

**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 9% strength reduction from lateral head tilt alone (Sokolov,
1967, a cited finding, not invented) is a concrete, citable reason to coach a neutral head
position during a maximal clean attempt, beyond generic "keep your head neutral" cueing.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Ch1, the general
torque/leverage principle this claim supplies specific joint-angle examples for);
[[principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal]] (the pelvis-specific continuation
of this same posture discussion, 3.3.4.2).

=== claim--pre-working-muscle-state-ranks-performance.md

# Muscle State Just Before a Movement Ranks Performance: Stretched > Contracted > Relaxed

**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
isometrically tensioned, or dynamically stretched) changes the working effect of the
subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose
across three pre-working conditions, besides the relaxed state, in this order: from a
static half-squat position 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ± 5.0 cm; and
after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for 10 milliseconds beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement, eliminating
*spurious* tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal
preliminary tension for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided
its duration is kept limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157,
printed pp. 144-146, "3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig
3.14.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly: "when a movement is begun with the muscles
relaxed, they are not optimally ready to work; consequently, they produce a smaller kinetic
effect than what they are capable of" (printed 145). **Inference:** the mechanism of "less
time/force spent simply activating the muscle" is this entry's own gloss, not the text's
wording. Preliminary tension is described (citing Bernstein) as the "anticipation tuner" of
the neuromuscular system, and a genuine stretch is stated to add banked elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction, plus reflexes that "increase the force of
muscle contractility as the afferent impulses increase in frequency and intensity" (printed
145).

**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or
lift outperforms a fully relaxed static start, and to caution against blanket "stay loose
and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for
Baylor's force-plate testing, this is consistent with running both a static-start (squat
jump) and a countermovement variant in the CMJ family (per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`; that family does not include a depth-jump variant),
since the pre-working state itself is shown here to be a first-order performance variable,
not just methodological noise.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific jump-height numbers (39.0/44.2/48.6 cm) come from one
Verkhoshansky dataset and should not be treated as universal benchmarks; the "stay relaxed"
qualification applies specifically to *spurious* tension in muscles unrelated to the task:
it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.

**Example** — **Inference:** a vertical-jump test protocol that only records a
static-squat-start jump will differ systematically from a depth-jump variant; the two
groups here differed by roughly 25% (39.0 to 48.6 cm), but Kozinc et al 2022 (vault,
`research-papers/kozinc-2022-...`) found only about 48.4% of 770 people jump clearly higher
in a countermovement jump than a squat jump, so individual variation is large and this
should not be read as a universal, individually-reliable difference. This example is not in
the source.

**Related** — [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (the same
depth-jump stimulus used as a measurement tool rather than a performance-boosting
pre-working state); [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Ch1, the
elastic-storage mechanism behind the stretched-state advantage).
=== framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial.md

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups), a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). For athletes who lift the same absolute load, distinguishing between
them requires calculating relative (bodymass-adjusted) static or dynamic strength-endurance;
this is stated for that specific comparison case, not as a general requirement for every
partial-endurance comparison. Elsewhere, in Chapter 2 (printed 108-109), the text names a
three-way classification: static, dynamic, and *explosive* strength-endurance (repetitively
executing explosive effort); this section (3.2.2) instead splits strength-endurance into
just static and dynamic, with no mention of an explosive form. The text does not reconcile
these two classifications, and this entry does not either. Strength-endurance's specificity
is stated as lower than speed's, "although its carry-over from one type of activity to
another is greater" (printed 142). (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp. 142-144, "3.2.2
Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The authors state only that different studies measured different
endurance types (printed 143), not a mechanism for why that produces opposite-signed
correlations. **Inference:** an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal
strength (a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while
a relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality; this mechanism is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests": this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — **Inference:** a quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a
whole roster measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the
same test at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric. This example is not in the
source. The text's own guidance is that the best way to develop strength-endurance is to
execute the competition exercises themselves under demanding conditions or in a large
volume, without excluding special strength exercises (printed 144).

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).
=== claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases.md

# Transfer Between Physical Qualities (Strength, Speed, Endurance) Shrinks as an Athlete's Specific Fitness Rises

**What it is** — Summarizing a body of Soviet and Western literature (Zimkin 1956/1965;
Zatsiorsky 1961/1965; Yakovlev et al 1960; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg 1949; Nelson 1957; Woodworth
1958; Cratty 1964, 1968; Cumbeca et al 1957; Bachman 1961; Lawther 1968; Barrow 1971;
Korobkov 1958), the authors report several established findings on how general physical
qualities (strength, speed, endurance) relate to each other over an athlete's development:
transference of physical qualities decreases as specific fitness increases; the transfer
mechanism is largely specific rather than general; the relationship between physical
qualities can be positive, negative, or neutral; and positive transfer between qualities in
early training can turn into negative transfer later (Korobkov, 1958). They also note it was
often claimed that complex training combining speed, strength, and endurance work develops
each quality better than training each individually (Ozolin, 1949, 1970), but state this
specific claim's validity is examined later in the book rather than settled here. The
following paragraph states a related but separate point, in tension with the above: "the
development of each quality positively influences the development of the others," and a lag
in developing one or more qualities "limits the development of the others" (Krestovnikov
1951; Kaledin 1961; printed 116). This is about qualities supporting each other's
development, not about transfer shrinking as specific fitness rises; the text does not
reconcile the two points, and this entry records both rather than picking one. (PDF pp.
127-128, printed pp. 116-117.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for why transfer specifically *decreases*
as specific fitness increases. The conditioned-reflex model of learned muscular activity is
given for the adjacent point above (why qualities support each other's development), not
for the transfer-decrease finding: training builds an extensive background of "temporary
connections" that different combinations of motor activity can later draw on; the text
states, as a training prescription rather than an observed fact, that "the training means
should develop the motor qualities separately" before combined work (printed 116).
**Inference:** the transfer-decrease finding itself is functionally consistent with the more
detailed ten-dimension specificity principle from Chapter 1 (see
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself; this link is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the authors themselves defer that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude. The authors themselves add a caution one page later: much of the
specificity literature draws on subjects of low sports qualification, sports mastery is not
accounted for, and conclusions "should be very cautious" and not generalized beyond the
athletes they were drawn from (printed 117).

**Example** — **Inference:** a young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and
conditioning work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general
strength and conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his
sport-specific qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to
be replaced by increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.
This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1);
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]]
(Bondarchuk's positive/negative/neutral transfer taxonomy, a compatible framing of the same
general topic).

[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]]), applied here at the coarser level of
whole physical qualities (strength/speed/endurance) rather than the ten specific training
dimensions within strength itself; this link is not stated in the text.

**When to apply** — Use this as the rationale for reducing reliance on general physical
qualities (e.g. general conditioning, general strength) as an athlete advances, and shifting
training emphasis toward sport-specific expressions of those qualities as specific fitness
rises. **Eric's baseline:** the department already sequences training from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk) rather than treating "sport specific" as a single category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this claim supports that same general-to-specific sequencing logic, and adds the caution that
positive transfer seen in an athlete's early training years should not be assumed to persist
unchanged as that athlete advances; a quality that helped early on can plateau in usefulness,
or even work against continued improvement, later.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the "complex training" question (whether training
speed, strength, and endurance together beats training them separately) is explicitly left
unresolved in this passage; do not cite this section as evidence for or against combined
training methods, since the authors themselves defer that judgment to later chapters not yet
ingested. This claim is also a summary of an older, mixed literature base spanning several
decades and traditions (1920s-1970s), not a single controlled study; treat the general
direction (transfer shrinks with rising specificity) as the useful takeaway rather than any
precise magnitude. The authors themselves add a caution one page later: much of the
specificity literature draws on subjects of low sports qualification, sports mastery is not
accounted for, and conclusions "should be very cautious" and not generalized beyond the
athletes they were drawn from (printed 117).

**Example** — **Inference:** a young multi-sport high-school athlete's general strength and
conditioning work is likely to transfer broadly across several sports; the same general
strength and conditioning work in a veteran college athlete already near the ceiling of his
sport-specific qualities is expected, per this claim, to transfer far less, and may need to
be replaced by increasingly sport- and position-specific training to keep producing gains.
This example is not in the source.

[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Chapter 1);
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]]
(Bondarchuk's positive/negative/neutral transfer taxonomy, a compatible framing of the same
general topic).

#### PDF 127 / printed 116
SUPERTRAINING
within reasonable limits to produce optimal results. In other words, it is the controlled achievement of the adaptive 
regularities which determines the character and dynamics of functional specialisation of the body during long-term 
special-strength training.
2.3 C haracteristics of Physical Fitness
Sports activity is characterised by the introduction of a physical regime to which the body is unaccustomed. The 
body attempts to accommodate to it with its entire complex of systems, including the central nervous, 
neuromuscular and muscular systems. Interaction between the various responses to these systems establishes the 
working efficiency of the body as a whole.
Thus, it is the form of the athlete’s physical fitness (i.e. the structural and functional adaptation of the body) 
that determines work capacity. The body’s work capacity acquires a certain specificity which depends on the type 
of sport. So, one can speak of the primary development of the ability to display qualities such as strength, speed 
and endurance, and call this key characteristic his motor function.
Each key function experiences a typical adaptation. 
It is largely inherent to any athlete of a given 
specialisation, although it can have an individual character in each case. Significantly distinct, individual differences 
can occur in the structure of strength fitness. 
Different athletes can obtain the same results using different 
contributions of work by the basic muscle groups, their different abilities to contract quickly, and their tendency 
to compensate for the functional lag of one muscle by more pronounced development of other muscles. Hence, the 
concept of the structure of strength fitness has great significance for organising strength training and especially for 
selecting effective means of developing muscular strength.
2.3.1 The Structure o f Physical Fitness
The concept of the structure of physical qualities in general, has been formulated in a number of studies, but only 
as a statement of the problems involved (Zatsiorsky, 1961, 1965; Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970, 1972). Until now a 
sufficiently thorough analysis has not been undertaken. At the same time, findings concerning the structure of 
physical fitness have been extensively covered in the literature, in particular concerning the interrelation between 
physical qualities (during their development); and the transfer of these qualities from one type of activity to 
another (Zimkin, 1965; Yakovlev et al, 1960; Zatsiorsky, 1965; Hebb 1949; Lindeburg, 1949; Nelson, 1957; 
Woodworth, 1958; Cratty, 1964). These studies have established that:
• The transference of physical qualities decreases with an increase in specific fitness (Zimkin, 1965; 
Zatsiorsky, 1965)
• The transference mechanism is to a great extent specific (Cumbeca et al 1957; Nelson 1957; Bachman, 1961;
Cratty, 1968; Lawther, 1968; Barrow, 1971)
• The interrelation between physical qualities can be positive, negative or neutral (Zimkin, 1956)
• Positive transference of certain qualities during the initial stages of training can lead later to negative 
transference (Korobkov, 1958).
It has often been claimed that complex training consisting of exercises which collectively involve speed, strength 
and endurance activities develops each of these qualities better than training each of them individually, even if the 
load is increased for the separate activities (Ozolin 1949, 1970). The validity of this assertion is examined later in 
this and later chapters.
The development of each quality positively influences the development of the others, and conversely, a lag in 
the development of one or more qualities limits the development o f the others (Krestovnikov, 1951; Kaledin. 
1961). For example, the development of strength and speed develops the ability to display speed-strength 
(Zimkin, 1956; Kuznetsov, 1970).
Here the theoretical explanation is based on the mechanism of the conditioned reflex which underlies learned 
muscular activity. Training leads to the formation of an extensive background of temporary connections, which 
serves as a foundation on which various combinations of the motor activities can arise, depending upon the 
emphasis of training. It is assumed that, in the beginning, the training means should develop the motor qualities 
separately. They are later integrated on the basis of the sports movements which are structurally similar to them.
Recent developments have supplemented the 1930s' concept of the specificity of human motor abilities, based 
upon considerable research (Downey, 1923; Allport, 1933; McCloy, 1937; Vcrkhoshansky, 1970, 1972). This
116


#### PDF 128 / printed 117
SUPERTRAINING
emphasizes the highly complex relationships between motor abilities, the development of various means for the 
different kinds of muscle activity, and the consequent low degree of generality, high degree of specificity and poor 
transference from one type of activity to another.
The existence of general and specific abilities supports this concept. General abilities form the basis for the 
ability to execute several different tasks, as they arc constant relative to any fluctuations of the conditions under 
which the task is executed. The general motor abilities provide the foundation for the execution of motor tasks and 
determine the relative stability of the neuromuscular system. They are regulated by heredity, physical structure 
and physiology.
Specific abilities reflect the functional specifics of performance in complex motor tasks, and are the chief 
results of motor experience gained by interaction with the environment. If general abilities facilitate the execution 
of several similar types o f task, then specific abilities will be largely independent, enhancing only one specific 
activity. 
Attempts have been made to formulate theories explaining the physiology of specificity and the 
functional independence of different motor abilities with respect to neuromuscular coordination (Pitts, 1954; 
Henkey, 1960; Henkey & Whitlec 1960; Smith, 1962). However, these attempts remain largely speculative, since 
they are based on fairly rudimentary research.
Despite numerous studies, much is still unclear and contradictory regarding the nature of strength abilities. 
.Analysis of the literature identifies some of the conclusions on which specialists generally tend to agree 
(Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972). In this respect, many articles assert that muscular strength developed by one 
means docs not have universal application, that there is no correlation between absolute muscular strength and 
speed of movement, that strength exercises decrease the speed of movement, that there is no relationship between 
static and dynamic strength, that there is no carry-over from isometric training to dynamic activity, and that 
dynamic strength relates more closely to motor performance than isometric strength.
However, it should be noted that such conclusions on the interrelation of motor abilities are often based on 
data obtained from subjects of low sports qualification and where the process of achieving sports mastery is not 
taken into consideration. It is therefore necessary to be very cautious about these conclusions and limit their 
applicability to those categories of athletes from which they were obtained and not to generalise prematurely.
The concept of the structure of an athlete's physical fitness (in particular, strength fitness) must be based on 
research and competitive performance. 
With respect to this, it is appropriate to distinguish between the 
composition and structure of the athlete's physical fitness (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The composition refers to the 
collection of all specific forms of the work capability which determine prowess in a given sport (e.g. strength, 
speed-strength, specd-endurance and other factors detailed in Section 1.15.4 and Table 8.1), whereas the structure 
refers to that complex interrelationship which functionally unites these independent motor abilities and determines 
the body's capability in that sport.
2.3.2 The Interrelation betw een Motor Abilities
Research enables us to recognise the following connections between motor abilities: general and partial, essential 
and non-essential, positive and negative, direct and indirect (Verkhoshansky, 1970, 1972 ; Scmyenov, 1971; 
Tatyan, 1974; Khodykin, 1976).
General and Partial C onnections
A general connection is characterised by the interaction between any two motor abilities, including the influence of 
all other abilities, whereas a partial connection involves only the indirect interaction between two abilities. 
Calculation of the general and partial correlations is used for quantitatively assessing these types of connections. 
Studies of the general and partial connections, using athletes of different specialisation and qualification have 
established that (Verkhoshansky, 1977):
1. Depending upon the abilities compared, the contribution of the partial connections can be lower (the most 
typical case) or higher than the contribution of the general connections.
2. The contribution of the partial connection between the same abilities in different sports is more stable than 
the contribution of the general connections.
Essential and N on-Essential C onnections
These connections are characterised to a greater or lesser extent by the interaction of the motor abilities in sport. 
Research indicates that essential connections (without which efficient sporting action is impossible) are more stable
117

Figure 2.21 (a) Increase in relative strength of the shoulder flexors (1), elbow extensors (2) and the abdominal muscles (3) of pok 
vaulters with growth of sports mastery, (b) Increase in rate o f change of relative strength relative to height achieved, for the same muse* 
groups of pole-vaulters. (Siff & Vcrkhoshansky, 1999).
This continuity is easily explained. Novice athletes raise their bodies up the pole with their abdominal muscles, 
but with increase in mastery, this raising is executed quickly by the arms and shoulders. The strength of these 
muscles increases significantly at the same time as the strength of the elbow extensors (2) increases uniformly.
In a study conducted by Vcrkhoshansky and Purvin, it was discovered that, with the growth of mastery in the 
shot put, the key role gradually shifts from the shoulder to the leg muscles (Verkhoshansky, 1977). For beginners, 
the correlation between athletic achievements and the strength of the arm muscles is 0.83, and with leg strength
0.37. The corresponding figures for highly qualified athletes are 0.73 and 0.87, respectively.
A more detailed analysis of the functional specialisation of the key muscle groups (in the example of jumpen 
and sprinters) also reveals the heterochronicity phenomenon. It appears in the given case in two forms:
• the non-coincidence of the initial rate of increase of specific strength factors (Fig 2.22a)
• the characteristic sequence of functional specialisation in the key mu
=========
#### PDF 154 / printed 143
SUPERTRAINING
one study found a general, positive correlation between strength and endurance, another discovered no such 
relationship, while a third observed a negative correlation. The reason for these discrepancies is that different 
endurance abilities usually are measured. Therefore, it has been suggested that endurance be classified into two 
types, in which the motor abilities refer to qualities such as static strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength 
and explosive strength. (Zatsiorsky et al, 1965):
• Absolute endurance, the overall result without considering the level of development of the individual motor 
abilities
• Partial endurance, the level of development of specific motor abilities calculated when the influence of other
abilities is in some way excluded.
Figure 3.12 Correlation model of special strength fitness of crawl stroke sprint swimmers (Verkhoshansky. 1977).
Thus, to determine partial endurance in strength exercises, a weight which requires exertion of a given percentage 
of one's maximal strength must be held (static strength-endurance) or moved repetitively to failure (dynamic 
strength-endurance). A partial index is obtained if there is either no correlation with maximal strength or a 
negative correlation. In the case where subjects raise the same weight, the assessment of absolute strength- 
endurance has a high positive correlation with maximal strength (Verkhoshansky, 1997). To distinguish between 
these subjects, it is then necessary to calculate relative static or dynamic strength-endurance by dividing the load 
lifted by bodymass or by a bodymass adjustment factor (see 3.3.5). As noted before, the contradictory eval­
uations of strength-endurance and its relationship to strength may be explained by the fact that some studies 
examined partial strength-endurance and others examined absolute strength-endurance.
Strength-endurance is as specific as the other characteristics of muscular activity. However, the specificity of 
strength-endurance is expressed to a lesser degree than, say, the specificity o f speed, although its carry-over from 
one type of activity to another is greater. One should remember that strength-endurance provides a high level of 
special work capacity that is mainly typical of cyclic types of sport and those involving the repetition of 
powerful actions (Verkhoshansky, 1997). In acyclic sports and chiefly those where technique and skill are
143


#### PDF 155 / printed 144
SUPERTRAINING
The hypothesis that special endurance (including strcngth-endurance) is developed from a preliminary base of 
general endurance is fairly universally accepted (see review by Nabatnikov, 1972). The best way to develop 
strcngth-endurance is to execute the competition exercises under demanding conditions or in a large volume. 
However, this does not exclude the use of special strength exercises.
In conclusion, it should be pointed out that an objective, reliable means of evaluating strength-endurance in 
sporting activity has not yet been devised. Specialists frequently use inadequate tests which diminish the value of 
the studies and produce contradictions. Therefore, the first condition to be met for eliminating deficiencies in the 
theory of sports training is to devise objective, consistent ways of evaluating strength-endurance.
3.3 Influence of External Conditions on Strength
Muscular force and consequently, the working effect of movement is influenced to a significant extent by external 
conditions, as well as by physiological and psychological factors.
3.3.1 The Influence of Pre-working State of the M uscles
The working effect of an athletic movement is determined largely by the state of the muscle prior to the 
production of force: it is important whether it is relaxed, contracted or stretched at the beginning of the action.
Under laboratory conditions, using model movements (e.g. throwing a load upward on a special machine), 
evaluation of the working effect (the height attained by the load) depends on the pre-working state of the 
neuromuscular system, as follows:
1. muscles relaxed
2. muscles in isometric tension produced by loading with various weights
3. muscles stretched dynamically, e.g. during the 'wave' phase in swimming
4. muscles stretched by 'shock' loading caused, e.g. by rapid braking of a load which has fallen from a height.
The results of an experiment (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977), shown graphically in terms of the distance (Sy), velocity 
(Vy) and acceleration (Ay) of a load, illustrates the growth of the working effect in switching from one thrust 
variant to another in the sequence shown (Fig 3.14).
In other experiments, the same type of prc-working state of muscle (besides the relaxed state) was 
reproduced in the take-off for the vertical jump. The subjects executed the vertical jump without arm movement,

important, the role of strength-endurance, especially the static form, is even more significant (depending upon 
one's level of sports proficiency).
For example (Fig 3.13), archers experience a steady increase in maximal strength, Fmax, and 
strength* 
endurance (judged from tmax, the time taken to reach maximal force). At the same time, the relationship between 
these indices and sporting results gradually decreases. In this case, it follows that the improvement in the results 
of highly qualified athletes (archers) is determined not so much by strength-cndurance as it is by the ability to 
control the muscular contraction necessary for stretching the bow-string (Farfel et al, 1975).


#### PDF 156 / printed 145
SUPERTRAINING
from a static half-squat position, after a preliminary half-squat and after a depth-jump from 0.5m. The heights 
attained were, respectively 39.0 ±  6.0 cm; 44.2 ±  5.0 cm and 48.6 ±  7.0 cm. (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970).
Thus, the muscle’s preliminary state appreciably influences the working effect of the movement. When the 
muscles are relaxed or in a state of isometric tension, the speed and power of their subsequent contraction is 
determined primarily by the nervous impulses to the muscles. If the muscles are subjected to a preliminary 
stretch by an external force, then the work they perform is further aided by some of the elastic energy which they 
have accumulated. Of considerable significance are the reflexes of the neuromuscular system, which increase the 
force of muscle contractility as the afferent impulses increase in frequency and intensity.
It is important here to examine the first type of pre-working state of muscle. It is frequently asserted that the 
muscles must be relaxed in the pre-working state and that this is an important indicator of the athlete's 
proficiency. However, this recommendation should not be generalised as being appropriate to every sports 
activity without considering the character of the movements and the situation.
Figure 3.14 The dynamics of a moving load for different pre-working states of muscle (the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 refer to the muscle 
flaics described in the preceding text). (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
It is known that the working force is preceded by some change in the muscles, particularly in the form of 
preliminary tension (the 'anticipation tuner' of the neuromuscular system, according to AV Bernstein). Great 
speed of movement has been noted with the sudden release of muscles from a state of full tetanus (Jewell & 
Wilkie, 1958). Under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, the subjects executed the movement 4% more 
rapidly, while the reaction time was seven times faster than in the relaxed state. The fastest reaction time and 
speed of movement indices correspond in order of effectiveness to the following preliminary muscle conditions: 
1. Stretched > 2. Contracted > 3. Relaxed (Smith, 1964). It was also demonstrated that the latent period of a 
motor reflex reaction is shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for 10 milliseconds (Person, 1965).
Research indicates that, when a movement is begun with the muscles relaxed, they are not optimally ready to 
work; consequently, they produce a smaller kinetic effect than what they are capable of. Clearly, preliminary 
muscular tension is not detrimental to performance, as is frequently stated in the literature: it is just the reverse, 
because an optimal magnitude can increase movement efficiency.
Therefore, preliminary relaxation should be understood to be relative to the specific movement. Relaxation, 
meaning the elimination of excessive or spurious muscular tension, is not directly related to the movement or the 
working of the muscles engaged in the passive phase of cyclic locomotion, but it is without a doubt an important

19:## Philosophy and decision principles
25:- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consi
26:- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
33:## Department model and roles
39:- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-
42:## Testing and assessment
44:- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
50:- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and p
51:- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM 
52:- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, cha
55:## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring
58:- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys
59:- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabi
60:- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protoco
61:- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how
62:- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover 
64:## Load monitoring and GPS
68:- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applie
71:- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data loo
73:## Speed and sprint
80:## Strength and power
83:- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + s
85:- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [0119202
86:- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build st
88:- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-tr
90:- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferr
92:## Conditioning and energy systems
100:- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary tra
104:- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp
106:## Rehab and return to play
111:- NordBord hamstring testing, dropped for roster-wide use, is explicitly retained for smaller, targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style). **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
115:## Injury risk and prevention
118:- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcri
122:## Recovery and sleep
127:## Nutrition and body composition
134:## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach
136:- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye." **Inferred (tra
143:## Periodization and programming
153:## Data, technology and reporting
155:- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-appl
157:- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflo
162:## Education and staff development
165:- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson

183:3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under
185:4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stac
189:6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very nex
193:8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring
201:## Named influences
208:| Anatoly Bondarchuk (transcribed as "Bondurciu") | General prep / specific prep / specific development / competitive exercise taxonomy | class1-transcript.md p.16; week1-lecture.md p.36 | Course material |
217:| Hawkin Dynamics | Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) metric-selection framework for force-plate reporting | hd-odsf-metrics.md | Vendor framework, adopted as practice |

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]

# Post-Tetanic Potentiation (the Book's "After-Effect"): Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

**Terminology note:** the text's own term is "post-tetanic potentiation" (a Western
physiology term for the phenomenon it calls the "after-effect"); this entry's original
title equated that with "post-activation potentiation." Modern usage generally
distinguishes post-tetanic potentiation (PTP), post-activation potentiation (PAP), and
post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) as related but not identical concepts
(no specific paper is cited here for that distinction; verify before citing one).

**What it is** — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent
activity is measurably altered, a phenomenon called (in Western physiology) post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters**: preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but with the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric), "results
deteriorate" (printed 164). The after-effect "occurs immediately after preliminary
isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still retains some trace of inhibitory
influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared with its
initial level" (printed 164). **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest
post-isometric dynamic-strength boost (90%, as printed; this sits beside 6.7% and 5.8% for
the other two loads tested and is a probable misprint, though recorded here as given) came
after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7% boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8%: "the
optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for obtaining the greatest post-work
improvement," though with rising fitness, larger loads (up to 100% max) can start producing
the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing window** depends on the conditioning
stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive isometric force rose 25% within the
first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5 minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped
2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for vertical jump specifically, barbell squats
potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes post, while depth jumps potentiated jump
height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes post. In a separate Ilin (1961) dataset on
preliminary isometric tension, "the maximum was achieved most rapidly with loads of 25% of
1RM (after 12 minutes), and most slowly with 100% of 1RM (after 15.4 minutes) and 50% of
1RM (after 17.2 minutes)," quoted as printed (printed 165): note the numbers themselves make
50% the slowest of the three to peak, not 100%, so the load-to-timing relationship is not
perfectly monotonic across every study cited, and this entry does not try to smooth that
over. The text also cautions that "over-excitation of the CNS has a negative effect on the
precision and coordination of movements," i.e. on athletic skill (printed 164). **Rest
interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not
(Klimonov, 1965). **Delayed effects**: moderate-volume barbell work produces a positive
tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect
by 5-6 days. (PDF pp. 175-178, printed pp. 164-166, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle
Activity," Figs 3.27-3.29.)

**Why it works** — The text frames this as a nervous-system "after-effect" or "trace"
phenomenon: any stimulus, momentary or not, leaves a lingering trace in the nervous system
reflecting its relative inertness, which is proposed as foundational to how fitness
continues rising despite periodic breaks in training. The text also separately states that
heavy dynamic work "elicits a positive after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS),
which produces a general toning influence on the motor apparatus." **Inference:** treating
the isometric-then-dynamic sequencing effect specifically as an instance of this same
central-trace/CNS-toning mechanism, rather than a purely local muscular effect, connects
two statements the text makes separately; the authors do not state this connection in one
sentence.

**When to apply** — Use this as a concrete, quantified starting template for complex/contrast
training design (heavy strength stimulus paired with an explosive movement): favor ~50% 1RM
isometric or heavy-tonic conditioning stimuli over maximal loads for athletes not yet highly
trained; expect the potentiation window to open within 1 minute and build over several
minutes, with the peak timing shifting later (toward 8-10 minutes) for a more demanding
stimulus like depth jumps versus barbell squats; and program the explosive/dynamic movement
*after* the conditioning stimulus, never the reverse order, per the sequencing finding.
**Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this offers a citable, historically-grounded
starting point (a squat-then-jump contrast pair with a 3-5 minute rest window) if the
department wants to formalize a PAP/complex-training protocol, to be validated against the
department's own force-plate (CMJ) data on actual athletes before being adopted as policy.

**When NOT to apply** — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies
(Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg
extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as
non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this
should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This
framework should be read alongside [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]],
which documents that Western studies of the same general phenomenon found much weaker or
absent effects: the sequencing/timing rules here reflect the Russian dataset specifically,
not a universally-replicated finding.

**Example** — **Inference:** a contrast-training set of back squats at ~50-60% 1RM followed
3-4 minutes later by depth jumps is a direct, testable application of this framework's load
and timing findings for a Baylor athlete; per the sequencing finding above, the dynamic
movement should come after the conditioning stimulus, never before it. Note that the 50%
figure in the load-response data above refers to a preliminary *static* effort's load
(e.g. an isometric squat hold), not necessarily a back-squat training load; treat the
percentage as illustrative of relative intensity, not a literal back-squat prescription.
This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines]] (the preceding
subsection on general warm-up, a related but distinct CNS-priming phenomenon);
[[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]] (the documented Western/Russian
disagreement on whether this effect reliably occurs at all).
