# Coach Head and Eye Position Deliberately During Barbell Lifts: It Drives Spinal Reflexes and Balance

**What it is** — Head position has a powerful, largely reflexive effect on posture and
lifting safety. Flexing the neck causes a **reflex relaxation of the back's erector
muscles**, which is dangerous during resisted lifts (squatting, cleaning, deadlifting), so
a deliberate degree of neck extension is needed to facilitate strong erector contraction
during ground-based pulls, but not so much as to hyperextend/hollow the back, which
loads the spinal discs asymmetrically. Rotation of the spine can be produced by rotation of
the head, so the head should also be kept in a straight-forward position during lifting;
head rotation is inadvisable not only during lifting from the ground but also during
supine loaded movements such as the bench press, where a backward-tilted head during the
lift can cause loaded cervical hyperextension and damage the neck's fragile structures.
During skilled Olympic-lift phases, specific head errors have specific consequences:
throwing the head back prematurely during the pull can pull the bar too far from the body;
tilting the head back during the jerk can cause the lift to be lost forward; tilting the
head back to look up at the bar during the snatch's low-squat fixation can cause the lifter
to fall backward and lose the lift; and dropping the head down during the squat can push
the lumbar spine into a hyperflexed, injury-risk position. Eye fixation is tied to head
position: maintaining the neutral spinal position is easiest when the eyes look almost
directly ahead and fixed on a distant object, and a coach or teammate moving in the
lifter's line of sight can disrupt this fixation and should be avoided during training and
competition. (PDF pp. 165-166, printed pp. 154-155, "3.3.4.3 The Effect of Head Position on
Strength.")

**Why it works** — The text states the mechanism directly for the neck-position part only:
neck flexion causes a reflex relaxation of the back's erector muscles, which undermines
trunk stabilization during a loaded lift, while extension is needed to facilitate strong
erector contraction. **Inference:** the text does not explain the eye-fixation guidance
through this same reflex, only that it is "essential" alongside head position; that the two
share one mechanism (gaze driving head position, which then drives the cervical reflex) is
this entry's own connecting inference, not a claim the authors make.

# Warm-Up Works Through Temperature and CNS Priming, and Its Value Is Event- and Training-Status-Specific

**What it is** — The warm-up has two components: **general** (raising the body's overall
functional potential) and **specific** (establishing the optimal relationship between the

psychological readying. **Temperature mechanism**: muscle contracts faster and more
intensely as temperature rises within a safe range, and electrical muscle activity rises
with body temperature (Golenhofen & Goptert 1958; Book & Golenhofen 1959); a hot shower
increases isometric endurance and cyclic-work speed/endurance by 7.5-9.0%; cooling to 18°C
shortens muscular work capacity 2-3x; massage does not change cyclic endurance but does
increase explosive-work power. **Activity-specific evidence**: active, intense warm-ups
(not moderate-intensity ones) effectively prepare for speed-strength/explosive work,
producing measured gains such as +1.0-4.5 cm in women's basketball jumps, up to +10 cm in
long jump, +400-700 N boxing punch force with 0.02-0.04 s faster striking time, and
correlation between rest interval and punch force rising from R=0.40 (no warm-up) to
R=0.62 (after warm-up). Franks' literature summary (cited via Williams, 1983) gives the
governing decision rules: high-intensity short-duration events (weightlifting, shotput)
benefit from warming up; vigorous warm-up can *hurt* endurance-sport performance; low-intensity/endurance
athletes gain little from warming up; direct warm-ups (task-similar activity) at moderate
intensity/duration help trained athletes in explosive sports but not necessarily untrained
ones; indirect warm-ups (unrelated activity, e.g. cycling, stretching) can help if kept
unstressful; nearly all studies showing warm-up as *detrimental* used untrained subjects
who could not tolerate high-intensity warm-ups; and strenuous, non-specific warm-ups can
interfere with motor-skill-dependent sports. Earlier in the same discussion the text also

not beneficial for strength production" (printed 163), which sits against Franks' point

# Post-Tetanic Potentiation (the Book's "After-Effect"): Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

physiology term for the phenomenon it calls the "after-effect"); this entry's original
title equated that with "post-activation potentiation." Modern usage generally

post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) as related but not identical concepts
(no specific paper is cited here for that distinction; verify before citing one).

activity is measurably altered, a phenomenon called (in Western physiology) post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters**: preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but with the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric), "results
deteriorate" (printed 164). The after-effect "occurs immediately after preliminary
isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still retains some trace of inhibitory
influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared with its
initial level" (printed 164). **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest
post-isometric dynamic-strength boost (90%, as printed; this sits beside 6.7% and 5.8% for
the other two loads tested and is a probable misprint, though recorded here as given) came
after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7% boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8%: "the
optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for obtaining the greatest post-work
improvement," though with rising fitness, larger loads (up to 100% max) can start producing
the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing window** depends on the conditioning
stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive isometric force rose 25% within the
first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5 minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped
2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for vertical jump specifically, barbell squats
potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes post, while depth jumps potentiated jump
height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes post. In a separate Ilin (1961) dataset on
preliminary isometric tension, "the maximum was achieved most rapidly with loads of 25% of
1RM (after 12 minutes), and most slowly with 100% of 1RM (after 15.4 minutes) and 50% of

precision and coordination of movements," i.e. on athletic skill (printed 164). **Rest
interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not

tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect

central-trace/CNS-toning mechanism, rather than a purely local muscular effect, connects

# Coach Head and Eye Position Deliberately During Barbell Lifts: It Drives Spinal Reflexes and Balance

lifting safety. Flexing the neck causes a **reflex relaxation of the back's erector
muscles**, which is dangerous during resisted lifts (squatting, cleaning, deadlifting), so
a deliberate degree of neck extension is needed to facilitate strong erector contraction
during ground-based pulls, but not so much as to hyperextend/hollow the back, which

the head, so the head should also be kept in a straight-forward position during lifting;
head rotation is inadvisable not only during lifting from the ground but also during
supine loaded movements such as the bench press, where a backward-tilted head during the
lift can cause loaded cervical hyperextension and damage the neck's fragile structures.

throwing the head back prematurely during the pull can pull the bar too far from the body;

head back to look up at the bar during the snatch's low-squat fixation can cause the lifter
to fall backward and lose the lift; and dropping the head down during the squat can push
the lumbar spine into a hyperflexed, injury-risk position. Eye fixation is tied to head
position: maintaining the neutral spinal position is easiest when the eyes look almost
directly ahead and fixed on a distant object, and a coach or teammate moving in the
lifter's line of sight can disrupt this fixation and should be avoided during training and
competition. (PDF pp. 165-166, printed pp. 154-155, "3.3.4.3 The Effect of Head Position on

prescription language in Baylor's own S&C programming and in the HHPR 5355 curriculum

strike time) are single old studies on specific populations (women's basketball, boxers,
long jumpers) and should be treated as illustrative magnitude, not as guaranteed or
individually-applicable gains. The Franks rules are themselves a literature summary from

should be applied as heuristics, not fixed thresholds.

# There Is No Single "Correct" Pelvic Tilt: The Right Tilt Depends on the Movement Phase

**What it is** — The pelvis is the key link between spine and lower extremities, and
inappropriate orientation can create an unstable or weak base and expose the lumbar discs
to injury, particularly under spinal flexion or flexion-plus-rotation. The text directly
challenges the common fitness-industry instruction that a single "correct" (usually
posterior) pelvic tilt applies to all movement: the generally recommended posterior pelvic
tilt is inappropriate for lifting loads from the ground, as confirmed by video, force-plate,
and EMG analysis of weightlifters and powerlifters. There is a correct **lumbar-pelvic
rhythm** in which the appropriate tilt changes synchronously through a lift (Cailliet,
1981). Using the "iliac crest" convention: **posterior pelvic tilt** is appropriate for
sit-ups or lifting objects above waist level; **anterior pelvic tilt** is the correct
rotation for squatting, lifting heavy loads off the floor, or toe-touching, and starting a
lift or squat with a *posterior* tilt is specifically flagged as dangerous, since it causes
lumbar flexion and exposes the discs. The pelvis actually rotates in three dimensions (X-axis =
anterior-posterior tilt; Z-axis = side-to-side iliac-crest rocking, natural in walking but
risky if it occurs during squatting, overhead pressing, or deadlifting; Y-axis = rotation
that occurs naturally in walking, running, throwing, and kicking, but is harmful to the
lumbar spine under high load or momentum, especially combined with rotation on other axes).
"Neutral" pelvic tilt is explicitly reframed as a *reference standard* for static
standing/sitting/walking, not automatically "the safest position for all movement." (PDF
pp. 164-166, printed pp. 153-155, "3.3.4.2 Strength, Safety and Pelvic Tilt," Fig 3.22.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly that the purpose of deliberate pelvic tilting
is to maintain neutral lumbar curvature as closely as possible, and that neutral pelvic
position is defined only for static standing, so it changes if the body shifts to leaning,
supine, prone, or other positions. **Inference:** connecting these statements into a single
causal chain, i.e. that a fixed pelvic position therefore cannot preserve neutral lumbar
curvature across different lifting phases and so the tilt itself must change to keep that
protective goal constant, is this entry's own synthesis of separate sentences in the text,
not a single sentence the authors themselves state.

**When to apply** — Use this to correct blanket "posterior pelvic tilt" or "brace neutral"
coaching cues applied identically to sit-ups and to floor-based lifts (deadlift, clean
pull, squat): the text's own biomechanical analysis argues these need opposite tilt cues.
**Eric's baseline:** directly relevant to Baylor's barbell coaching (clean, snatch, squat,
deadlift patterns referenced in `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this gives a specific, citable rationale for differentiating tilt cues by lift and by
phase rather than using one universal cue for any staff in-service on lifting technique.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own synthesis (the text does not name a single
author for this passage) built primarily on one cited source (Cailliet, 1981) plus general
biomechanical reasoning, not a randomized or outcome-controlled study of injury rates under
different tilt cues; treat the specific "posterior tilt for sit-ups, anterior tilt for
squats/deadlifts" rule as a reasoned coaching heuristic backed by video/EMG description, not
as a proven injury-prevention intervention with measured outcomes. **Inference:** modern
spine-health research has questioned how directly lumbar flexion during lifting predicts
low back pain, which would narrow how strongly this section's injury-risk framing should be
read (no specific paper is cited here; verify before citing one). It also does not address
every possible lifting pattern (e.g. Olympic pulling positions), where the same reasoning
would need to be worked through separately.

**Example** — **Inference:** cueing a lifter to "tuck the pelvis under" (posterior tilt) at
the start of a deadlift or squat, following generic core-bracing advice borrowed from
ab-training cues, is exactly the error this section warns against. The text argues that
specific setup should use an anterior tilt at the iliac crest instead. This framing as a
coaching error is not stated in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (the preceding
subsection's general posture-and-force-output findings); [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]
(the next subsection's continuation of the same postural-safety discussion).

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate: coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed p. 155, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes. **Inference:** a
further reason, not stated in this section, is that isokinetic symmetry testing measures an
isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent functional, whole-movement asymmetry
accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply (direct tension with current Baylor practice)** — This claim sits in
tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection model
lists symmetry (L/R differences) as an *optional* force-plate reporting category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style) is retained
for targeted return-to-play groups (`method-baseline.md`, citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). The baseline does not itself say symmetry
indices *drive* RTP decisions, only that they are collected as an optional category and
that joint-specific testing continues for RTP groups; this entry should not be read as
claiming the baseline directly contradicts the book on that specific point. **Eric's review
would be needed** to reconcile this 1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based
"correction" with the department's practice: the book's objection is specifically to
*using an isokinetic ratio to drive a correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry
monitoring for tracking purposes more broadly. Modern literature is itself split on how
symmetry data should be used: Afonso et al (vault, `research-papers/afonso-undated-...`)
and Bishop 2016 (vault, `research-papers/bishop-2016-...`) both caution against naive
asymmetry-correction approaches, while Callaway 2026 (vault,
`research-papers/callaway-2026-...`) argues group-normative asymmetry thresholds fail to
represent individual players, a related but distinct caution about the metric itself
rather than about correcting it.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy,
high-performing athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not
automatically something to "fix": the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a
natural, individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (the preceding
subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); Ch4.2.8 "The Concept of Symmetric
Training" (explicitly deferred by the text itself, not yet ingested, future chapter).

chapter: "3.3.5"
confidence: supported

# Allometric Scaling Laws Let You Compare Strength Fairly Across Bodymass (and Height) Classes

**What it is** — Because bodymass scales with the cube of linear body dimensions while
muscle cross-sectional area (and thus force capacity) scales only with the square, maximum
strength (F) and bodymass (B) are theoretically related by F = a.B^(2/3) (Lietzke, 1956,
found a best-fit exponent of 0.6748, close to the theoretical 0.6667). Historical
weight-class-comparison formulas built on this (Hoffman's two-thirds-power formula, the
Austin 3/4-exponent formula, McSorley's and Sinclair's parabolic tables) each had accuracy
limits, especially extrapolating to heavier lifters. Siff (1988) fit sigmoid/power-law
curves to the mean of the ten best all-time lifts per bodymass class (up to ~165 kg) and
found a power-law equation, **Total T = a - b.B^(-c)**, fit weightlifting and powerlifting
records with R 0.996-0.999 (distinct constants given for weightlifting total,
powerlifting total, squat, bench, and deadlift); separate equations were fit for juvenile
lifters (logistic form) and for women (exponential form). Using these equations, an
athlete's Total can be expressed as a percentage of the world-class total for their exact
bodymass, enabling fair cross-weight-class comparison and longitudinal tracking even as an
athlete's bodymass itself changes. Analysis of the equations shows **relative strength
(strength per unit bodymass) actually peaks at a bodymass of 60-67 kg** in elite
weightlifters/powerlifters, not at either extreme. A related but weaker relationship: for a
given bodymass, taller lifters tend to be *less* strong at elite level (an exponential
height-bodymass equation is given per build class, Table 3.5); and the bodymass-strength
correlation weakens as movement speed increases (0.719 for the slow press vs. 0.706 clean-and-jerk
vs. 0.685 snatch), meaning bodymass predicts maximal-strength lifts much better than
fast, technical ones. (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 155-160, "3.3.5 The Dependence of
Strength on Bodymass," "3.3.6 The Relationship between Strength and Height," Tables 3.3-3.5,
Figs 3.23-3.24.)

**Why it works** — The scaling logic is dimensional analysis, not an empirical fit per se:
strength derives from muscle cross-sectional area (a squared, two-dimensional quantity)
while bodymass derives from volume (a cubed, three-dimensional quantity) for
geometrically-similar bodies, so absolute strength cannot keep pace linearly with bodymass
as size increases. This is the authors' own stated reasoning for the F=a.B^(2/3) relationship.
**Inference:** the text does not itself connect this same cross-sectional-area argument to
the separate height finding (3.3.6) in one sentence; extending the logic that way (a
taller lifter at a fixed bodymass has a thinner build and less muscle cross-section) is
this entry's own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make directly. The text separately
notes that both Krestovnikov (1939), Knipst (1952), Chudinov (1961), Zatsiorsky (1966) and
Martirosov et al (1967) observed relative strength decreasing as bodymass rises, "although
just the opposite finding has also been reported (Abramovsky, 1966)" (printed 158); this
entry records both rather than resolving the conflict. The authors also give a supporting
reason for using bodymass-adjustment equations rather than raw relative strength (load
divided by bodymass) for cross-athlete comparison: relative strength "is scientifically
preferable to reserve ... for assessing changes in an individual with time," while
comparing different individuals' bodymass is "far more accurate by applying the adjustment
equations" (printed 107).

**When to apply** — Use the underlying two-thirds-power scaling logic (a dimensional-analysis
argument the authors themselves give, not an appeal to outside literature this entry can
name) whenever normalizing strength testing data across athletes of different
bodymass, e.g. comparing back-squat 1RM across a football roster spanning 180-320+ lb
linemen to skill players is misleading without some bodymass adjustment, and simple
per-kg relative strength (load/bodymass) is itself an approximation that over- or
under-corrects depending where an athlete sits on this curve. **Eric's baseline** names
sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data as unfinished, prioritized work
(`performance-playbook-development-plan.md` 3.2.3). **Inference:** a bodymass-adjusted
strength-comparison method, even a simplified version of Siff's approach, would be a
concrete way to build fairer cross-position strength benchmarks for football specifically;
this specific application is not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific numeric constants (a, b, c values) are fit to
weightlifting and powerlifting records through 1987-1988 and to Russian weightlifter height
data of that era: they should not be applied directly to football or other sport
populations without refitting to relevant data. The dimensional-analysis argument for the
two-thirds exponent is general reasoning the authors give, but Lietzke's best-fit exponent
(0.6748) and Siff's regression constants are single-dataset fits; the "60-67 kg
relative-strength peak" finding is specific to Olympic/power lifters of that period and
should be treated as illustrative, not directly transferable without refitting.

**Example** — **Inference:** comparing a 90 kg lifter's 405 kg powerlifting total to a
139 kg lifter's 500 kg total (139 kg is the top bodymass row in Table 3.3) by raw numbers
alone favors the heavier lifter; converting each to a percentage of the world-class total
expected at their own bodymass (via Table 3.3's fitted curve) gives a fairer
relative-strength comparison, which is the entire point of this scaling approach. This
example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations]] (the next
subsection's parallel age-adjustment method, explicitly combined with this bodymass
adjustment in the book's own worked example); [[claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass]]
(uses the same bodymass-normalization logic for sex comparison).

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases**: 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7), meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, and hip flexors/extensors and knee
flexors/masticating muscles tied at 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any groups tested;
verified directly against the PDF page image, see `_book.md` process note on the
text-extraction discrepancy for this value). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed p.
161, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven mainly by
*how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any difference
in muscle tissue quality. **Inference:** the text separately notes the muscle-group ratios
"probably" reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between average men and women,
but it does not itself connect that habitual-use explanation to the specific pattern of
which muscle groups show the largest and smallest sex gaps (elbow flexors/extensors lowest
at 0.55, hip flexors/extensors highest at 0.80); that specific connection is this entry's
own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make sentence-by-sentence.

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes: the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline** defaults
women's-sport strength testing to repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols because
rep-max protocols are better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for
smaller-framed lifters (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18`, `week1-lecture.md p.39`; that stated reason is
tolerability, not sex-strength ratios). **Inference:** this table gives a separate,
physiological rationale for why a single sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across
different lifts/muscle groups if the department ever wanted to build sex-specific
relative-strength benchmarks by exercise; that specific application is not stated in the
baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously:
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every
exercise would overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there
(0.55) and underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap
(0.80), per Table 3.8. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).

---
chapter: "3.3.9"
confidence: supported
---

# Elite Lifting Performance Rose Steadily by Decade (Gompertz Curve); the Press's Faster Growth May Reflect Steroid Use

**What it is** — Normalizing weightlifting performance across all bodymass divisions (as a
percentage of the mean of the ten heaviest totals ever recorded per division, via the
bodymass-scaling equation from 3.3.5) and plotting the result by year from 1950-1990 shows a
**Gompertz growth curve** (Points y = a.e^(-b.e^(-cx)), x = year-1950) fits the historical
rise in performance well for the snatch, clean-and-jerk, and press (R = 0.994-0.996 for
each, with separate fitted constants a, b, c per lift). The snatch and clean-and-jerk show a
similar growth trend, but the **press grew measurably faster**. Since the Olympic press was
removed from competition in 1971, its longer-term trend cannot be studied further. (PDF pp.
172-173, printed pp. 161-162, "3.3.9 The Increase in Human Strength over Time," Fig 3.26.)

**Why it works** — The text states only that the Gompertz form is "commonly used by
actuaries and biologists to describe growth or decay processes" (printed 162). **Inference:**
that it fits generic athletic-record progression patterns with an early accelerating phase
and a plateau, rather than something specific to strength physiology, is this entry's own
gloss on that one sentence. For the *differential* growth rate between lifts, the text
offers an explicitly labeled interpretation, not a proven mechanism: Siff and Medvedev
"have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic
substances since the late 1950s," reasoning that the press is slower, more
quasi-isometric, and more dependent on muscle hypertrophy and relative strength than the
more technically-demanding snatch and clean-and-jerk, and that anabolic substances would be
expected to preferentially benefit hypertrophy-dependent, technically-simpler lifts (also
naming the powerlifting squat, bench press, and deadlift as lifts that would be expected to
benefit similarly).

**When to apply** — The Gompertz-curve secular-trend finding itself is useful background for
understanding why raw historical strength-record comparisons across decades are misleading
without normalizing for era; the steroid explanation should be treated and cited
specifically as **Siff and Medvedev's hypothesis**, a speculative interpretation of a
correlational pattern (different growth rates for different lifts), not as an established
causal finding.

**When NOT to apply** — The steroid-use explanation is explicitly hedged by Siff and
Medvedev themselves ("it is reasonable to expect...") and is not a tested causal claim: no
doping prevalence data, testing records, or controlled comparison is presented to support it
directly; it should be reported as Siff and Medvedev's inference from an indirect pattern
(differential growth rates by lift type), never as a confirmed finding. The Gompertz fit
itself is also a single dataset ending in 1990 and should not be extrapolated to predict
current-era performance ceilings without updated data. Separately, the text claims these
equations can be used not just to describe the past trend but to "predict increase both in
weightlifting performance and human strength over an extended period of time ... and also
to plan the desired improvements for the individual" (printed 162); treat that predictive
and individual-planning use with the same caution as the trend-fit itself, since it is
asserted, not independently validated here.

**Example** — Citing "weightlifting has improved steadily since 1950 per a Gompertz growth
model" is a supportable, quantified historical claim; citing "the press grew faster because
of steroids" as an established fact (rather than "Siff and Medvedev's own hypothesis, based
on the press's lower technical demand") would overstate what this section actually shows.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the same normalization method
used to build this secular-trend dataset).

challenges the common fitness-industry instruction that a single "correct" (usually
posterior) pelvic tilt applies to all movement: the generally recommended posterior pelvic
tilt is inappropriate for lifting loads from the ground, as confirmed by video, force-plate,
and EMG analysis of weightlifters and powerlifters. There is a correct **lumbar-pelvic
rhythm** in which the appropriate tilt changes synchronously through a lift (Cailliet,
1981). Using the "iliac crest" convention: **posterior pelvic tilt** is appropriate for
sit-ups or lifting objects above waist level; **anterior pelvic tilt** is the correct
rotation for squatting, lifting heavy loads off the floor, or toe-touching, and starting a
lift or squat with a *posterior* tilt is specifically flagged as dangerous, since it causes
lumbar flexion and exposes the discs. The pelvis actually rotates in three dimensions (X-axis =
anterior-posterior tilt; Z-axis = side-to-side iliac-crest rocking, natural in walking but
risky if it occurs during squatting, overhead pressing, or deadlifting; Y-axis = rotation
that occurs naturally in walking, running, throwing, and kicking, but is harmful to the
lumbar spine under high load or momentum, especially combined with rotation on other axes).
"Neutral" pelvic tilt is explicitly reframed as a *reference standard* for static
standing/sitting/walking, not automatically "the safest position for all movement." (PDF
pp. 164-166, printed pp. 153-155, "3.3.4.2 Strength, Safety and Pelvic Tilt," Fig 3.22.)

**Why it works** — The text states directly that the purpose of deliberate pelvic tilting
is to maintain neutral lumbar curvature as closely as possible, and that neutral pelvic
position is defined only for static standing, so it changes if the body shifts to leaning,
supine, prone, or other positions. **Inference:** connecting these statements into a single
causal chain, i.e. that a fixed pelvic position therefore cannot preserve neutral lumbar
curvature across different lifting phases and so the tilt itself must change to keep that
protective goal constant, is this entry's own synthesis of separate sentences in the text,
not a single sentence the authors themselves state.

**When to apply** — Use this to correct blanket "posterior pelvic tilt" or "brace neutral"
coaching cues applied identically to sit-ups and to floor-based lifts (deadlift, clean
pull, squat): the text's own biomechanical analysis argues these need opposite tilt cues.
**Eric's baseline:** directly relevant to Baylor's barbell coaching (clean, snatch, squat,
deadlift patterns referenced in `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`, `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`). **Inference:**
this gives a specific, citable rationale for differentiating tilt cues by lift and by
phase rather than using one universal cue for any staff in-service on lifting technique.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own synthesis (the text does not name a single
author for this passage) built primarily on one cited source (Cailliet, 1981) plus general
biomechanical reasoning, not a randomized or outcome-controlled study of injury rates under
different tilt cues; treat the specific "posterior tilt for sit-ups, anterior tilt for
squats/deadlifts" rule as a reasoned coaching heuristic backed by video/EMG description, not
as a proven injury-prevention intervention with measured outcomes. **Inference:** modern
spine-health research has questioned how directly lumbar flexion during lifting predicts
low back pain, which would narrow how strongly this section's injury-risk framing should be
read (no specific paper is cited here; verify before citing one). It also does not address
every possible lifting pattern (e.g. Olympic pulling positions), where the same reasoning
would need to be worked through separately.

**Example** — **Inference:** cueing a lifter to "tuck the pelvis under" (posterior tilt) at
the start of a deadlift or squat, following generic core-bracing advice borrowed from
ab-training cues, is exactly the error this section warns against. The text argues that
specific setup should use an anterior tilt at the iliac crest instead. This framing as a
coaching error is not stated in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (the preceding
subsection's general posture-and-force-output findings); [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]
(the next subsection's continuation of the same postural-safety discussion).

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate: coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed p. 155, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes. **Inference:** a
further reason, not stated in this section, is that isokinetic symmetry testing measures an
isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent functional, whole-movement asymmetry
accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply (direct tension with current Baylor practice)** — This claim sits in
tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection model
lists symmetry (L/R differences) as an *optional* force-plate reporting category
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style) is retained
for targeted return-to-play groups (`method-baseline.md`, citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). The baseline does not itself say symmetry
indices *drive* RTP decisions, only that they are collected as an optional category and
that joint-specific testing continues for RTP groups; this entry should not be read as
claiming the baseline directly contradicts the book on that specific point. **Eric's review
would be needed** to reconcile this 1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based
"correction" with the department's practice: the book's objection is specifically to
*using an isokinetic ratio to drive a correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry
monitoring for tracking purposes more broadly. Modern literature is itself split on how
symmetry data should be used: Afonso et al (vault, `research-papers/afonso-undated-...`)
and Bishop 2016 (vault, `research-papers/bishop-2016-...`) both caution against naive
asymmetry-correction approaches, while Callaway 2026 (vault,
`research-papers/callaway-2026-...`) argues group-normative asymmetry thresholds fail to
represent individual players, a related but distinct caution about the metric itself
rather than about correcting it.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy,
high-performing athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not
automatically something to "fix": the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a
natural, individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (the preceding
subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); Ch4.2.8 "The Concept of Symmetric
Training" (explicitly deferred by the text itself, not yet ingested, future chapter).

---
chapter: "3.3.5"
confidence: supported

# Allometric Scaling Laws Let You Compare Strength Fairly Across Bodymass (and Height) Classes

**What it is** — Because bodymass scales with the cube of linear body dimensions while
muscle cross-sectional area (and thus force capacity) scales only with the square, maximum
strength (F) and bodymass (B) are theoretically related by F = a.B^(2/3) (Lietzke, 1956,
found a best-fit exponent of 0.6748, close to the theoretical 0.6667). Historical
weight-class-comparison formulas built on this (Hoffman's two-thirds-power formula, the
Austin 3/4-exponent formula, McSorley's and Sinclair's parabolic tables) each had accuracy
limits, especially extrapolating to heavier lifters. Siff (1988) fit sigmoid/power-law
curves to the mean of the ten best all-time lifts per bodymass class (up to ~165 kg) and
found a power-law equation, **Total T = a - b.B^(-c)**, fit weightlifting and powerlifting
records with R 0.996-0.999 (distinct constants given for weightlifting total,
powerlifting total, squat, bench, and deadlift); separate equations were fit for juvenile
lifters (logistic form) and for women (exponential form). Using these equations, an
athlete's Total can be expressed as a percentage of the world-class total for their exact
bodymass, enabling fair cross-weight-class comparison and longitudinal tracking even as an
athlete's bodymass itself changes. Analysis of the equations shows **relative strength
(strength per unit bodymass) actually peaks at a bodymass of 60-67 kg** in elite
weightlifters/powerlifters, not at either extreme. A related but weaker relationship: for a
given bodymass, taller lifters tend to be *less* strong at elite level (an exponential
height-bodymass equation is given per build class, Table 3.5); and the bodymass-strength
correlation weakens as movement speed increases (0.719 for the slow press vs. 0.706 clean-and-jerk
vs. 0.685 snatch), meaning bodymass predicts maximal-strength lifts much better than
fast, technical ones. (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 155-160, "3.3.5 The Dependence of
Strength on Bodymass," "3.3.6 The Relationship between Strength and Height," Tables 3.3-3.5,
Figs 3.23-3.24.)

**Why it works** — The scaling logic is dimensional analysis, not an empirical fit per se:
strength derives from muscle cross-sectional area (a squared, two-dimensional quantity)
while bodymass derives from volume (a cubed, three-dimensional quantity) for
geometrically-similar bodies, so absolute strength cannot keep pace linearly with bodymass
as size increases. This is the authors' own stated reasoning for the F=a.B^(2/3) relationship.
**Inference:** the text does not itself connect this same cross-sectional-area argument to
the separate height finding (3.3.6) in one sentence; extending the logic that way (a
taller lifter at a fixed bodymass has a thinner build and less muscle cross-section) is
this entry's own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make directly. The text separately
notes that both Krestovnikov (1939), Knipst (1952), Chudinov (1961), Zatsiorsky (1966) and
Martirosov et al (1967) observed relative strength decreasing as bodymass rises, "although
just the opposite finding has also been reported (Abramovsky, 1966)" (printed 158); this
entry records both rather than resolving the conflict. The authors also give a supporting
reason for using bodymass-adjustment equations rather than raw relative strength (load
divided by bodymass) for cross-athlete comparison: relative strength "is scientifically
preferable to reserve ... for assessing changes in an individual with time," while
comparing different individuals' bodymass is "far more accurate by applying the adjustment
equations" (printed 107).

**When to apply** — Use the underlying two-thirds-power scaling logic (a dimensional-analysis
argument the authors themselves give, not an appeal to outside literature this entry can
name) whenever normalizing strength testing data across athletes of different
bodymass, e.g. comparing back-squat 1RM across a football roster spanning 180-320+ lb
linemen to skill players is misleading without some bodymass adjustment, and simple
per-kg relative strength (load/bodymass) is itself an approximation that over- or
under-corrects depending where an athlete sits on this curve. **Eric's baseline** names
sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data as unfinished, prioritized work
(`performance-playbook-development-plan.md` 3.2.3). **Inference:** a bodymass-adjusted
strength-comparison method, even a simplified version of Siff's approach, would be a
concrete way to build fairer cross-position strength benchmarks for football specifically;
this specific application is not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific numeric constants (a, b, c values) are fit to
weightlifting and powerlifting records through 1987-1988 and to Russian weightlifter height
data of that era: they should not be applied directly to football or other sport
populations without refitting to relevant data. The dimensional-analysis argument for the
two-thirds exponent is general reasoning the authors give, but Lietzke's best-fit exponent
(0.6748) and Siff's regression constants are single-dataset fits; the "60-67 kg
relative-strength peak" finding is specific to Olympic/power lifters of that period and
should be treated as illustrative, not directly transferable without refitting.

**Example** — **Inference:** comparing a 90 kg lifter's 405 kg powerlifting total to a
139 kg lifter's 500 kg total (139 kg is the top bodymass row in Table 3.3) by raw numbers
alone favors the heavier lifter; converting each to a percentage of the world-class total
expected at their own bodymass (via Table 3.3's fitted curve) gives a fairer
relative-strength comparison, which is the entire point of this scaling approach. This
example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations]] (the next
subsection's parallel age-adjustment method, explicitly combined with this bodymass
adjustment in the book's own worked example); [[claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass]]
(uses the same bodymass-normalization logic for sex comparison).

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases**: 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7), meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, and hip flexors/extensors and knee
flexors/masticating muscles tied at 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any groups tested;
verified directly against the PDF page image, see `_book.md` process note on the
text-extraction discrepancy for this value). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed p.
161, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven mainly by
*how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any difference
in muscle tissue quality. **Inference:** the text separately notes the muscle-group ratios
"probably" reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between average men and women,
but it does not itself connect that habitual-use explanation to the specific pattern of
which muscle groups show the largest and smallest sex gaps (elbow flexors/extensors lowest
at 0.55, hip flexors/extensors highest at 0.80); that specific connection is this entry's
own extrapolation, not a claim the authors make sentence-by-sentence.

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes: the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline** defaults
women's-sport strength testing to repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols because
rep-max protocols are better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for
smaller-framed lifters (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18`, `week1-lecture.md p.39`; that stated reason is
tolerability, not sex-strength ratios). **Inference:** this table gives a separate,
physiological rationale for why a single sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across
different lifts/muscle groups if the department ever wanted to build sex-specific
relative-strength benchmarks by exercise; that specific application is not stated in the
baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously:
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every
exercise would overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there
(0.55) and underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap
(0.80), per Table 3.8. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).

# Elite Lifting Performance Rose Steadily by Decade (Gompertz Curve); the Press's Faster Growth May Reflect Steroid Use

**What it is** — Normalizing weightlifting performance across all bodymass divisions (as a
percentage of the mean of the ten heaviest totals ever recorded per division, via the
bodymass-scaling equation from 3.3.5) and plotting the result by year from 1950-1990 shows a
**Gompertz growth curve** (Points y = a.e^(-b.e^(-cx)), x = year-1950) fits the historical
rise in performance well for the snatch, clean-and-jerk, and press (R = 0.994-0.996 for
each, with separate fitted constants a, b, c per lift). The snatch and clean-and-jerk show a
similar growth trend, but the **press grew measurably faster**. Since the Olympic press was
removed from competition in 1971, its longer-term trend cannot be studied further. (PDF pp.
172-173, printed pp. 161-162, "3.3.9 The Increase in Human Strength over Time," Fig 3.26.)

**Why it works** — The text states only that the Gompertz form is "commonly used by
actuaries and biologists to describe growth or decay processes" (printed 162). **Inference:**
that it fits generic athletic-record progression patterns with an early accelerating phase
and a plateau, rather than something specific to strength physiology, is this entry's own
gloss on that one sentence. For the *differential* growth rate between lifts, the text
offers an explicitly labeled interpretation, not a proven mechanism: Siff and Medvedev
"have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic
substances since the late 1950s," reasoning that the press is slower, more
quasi-isometric, and more dependent on muscle hypertrophy and relative strength than the
more technically-demanding snatch and clean-and-jerk, and that anabolic substances would be
expected to preferentially benefit hypertrophy-dependent, technically-simpler lifts (also
naming the powerlifting squat, bench press, and deadlift as lifts that would be expected to
benefit similarly).

**When to apply** — The Gompertz-curve secular-trend finding itself is useful background for
understanding why raw historical strength-record comparisons across decades are misleading
without normalizing for era; the steroid explanation should be treated and cited
specifically as **Siff and Medvedev's hypothesis**, a speculative interpretation of a
correlational pattern (different growth rates for different lifts), not as an established
causal finding.

**When NOT to apply** — The steroid-use explanation is explicitly hedged by Siff and
Medvedev themselves ("it is reasonable to expect...") and is not a tested causal claim: no
doping prevalence data, testing records, or controlled comparison is presented to support it
directly; it should be reported as Siff and Medvedev's inference from an indirect pattern
(differential growth rates by lift type), never as a confirmed finding. The Gompertz fit
itself is also a single dataset ending in 1990 and should not be extrapolated to predict
current-era performance ceilings without updated data. Separately, the text claims these
equations can be used not just to describe the past trend but to "predict increase both in
weightlifting performance and human strength over an extended period of time ... and also
to plan the desired improvements for the individual" (printed 162); treat that predictive
and individual-planning use with the same caution as the trend-fit itself, since it is
asserted, not independently validated here.

**Example** — Citing "weightlifting has improved steadily since 1950 per a Gompertz growth
model" is a supportable, quantified historical claim; citing "the press grew faster because
of steroids" as an established fact (rather than "Siff and Medvedev's own hypothesis, based
on the press's lower technical demand") would overstate what this section actually shows.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the same normalization method
used to build this secular-trend dataset).

=== framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type.md
---
chapter: "2.1.1"
confidence: supported
---

# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) changes in
a consistent three-stage sequence (Fig 2.3, printed pp. 98-99): (1) initially a relatively
uniform increase in force with an insignificant decrease in duration; (2) then a significant
increase in maximum force with a noticeable decrease in duration; (3) finally an increase in
the force developed at the beginning of the effort, with some further increase in maximum
and a decrease in the time taken to reach it. The overall pattern this leaves is: the time to
reach maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves
closer to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases; the
same printed-100 summary also lists an increase in the working amplitude of the movement as
part of this general pattern (see the SSC sub-pattern below, which instead reports a
decrease). The authors report longitudinal data from one individual (Fig 2.2, a seated leg
task, before and after 6 months of strength training, captioned Siff & Verkhoshansky 1999)
and cite several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
corroborating support (PDF pp. 109-110, printed pp. 98-99, Figs 2.1-2.3). The authors then
describe four distinct sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend
but differing in where force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which *decreases* the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows, the opposite direction from the general pattern's amplitude increase
  above; the text does not reconcile the two, and this entry does not either.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 110-111, printed pp. 99-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; they attribute it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is plausibly explained by task constraints (available time, external
resistance, and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of
the range the nervous system learns to emphasize; no citation is offered for this and none
is added here.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — **Inference:** a running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an
off-season block, would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more
front-loaded braking phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength
improves, distinct from an offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or
isometric mid-thigh pull trace) would be expected to show a rising peak force with a
flatter, less time-compressed profile. Neither example is in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1),

the stretch-shortening pattern here).

# Three Levels for Analyzing a Movement: Kinematic Pair, Kinematic Chain, Kinematic System

**What it is** — The authors organize movement analysis into three nested levels of
increasing complexity (PDF pp. 112-116, printed pp. 101-105): the **kinematic pair** (a
single joint, or two actively combined adjacent links, e.g. isolated knee extension), the
**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base). Two resulting-force-less-than-sum examples the text flags
as not yet adequately analysed in the sporting literature (printed 103-104): (a) in
isolated elbow flexion, strength peaks isometrically near 90 degrees, but with simultaneous
shoulder extension and elbow flexion (stretching work), maximum isometric force shifts to
about 160 degrees at the elbow, and with propulsive work through the whole upper extremity,
maximal force develops with the elbow near full flexion, near the beginning of the push-off
(Campney & Wehr 1965); (b) with isolated knee extension, maximal force occurs in the
80-130 degree range, but with propulsive work through hip and knee together, maximal force
occurs near full hip extension and a knee angle close to 160 degrees (Dorofeyev 1965;
Yegorov 1966). At the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms extend across a larger
number of interacting muscle groups; "the only difference is in the number of functionally
interacting muscle groups," involving chiefly the strongest muscle groups of the legs and
torso, followed by the shoulder girdle. The process of perfecting movement from the
kinematic-pair level to the system level "is closely associated with the efficient
organisation and control of the motor action" (printed 105).

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, they attribute the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level; Semyenov and Tatyanov (1976, printed 104) found a smaller
correlation between running and jumping performance and individual joint torques of the
lower extremity than between that performance and the force produced by the whole limb, a
correlation that strengthens further with proficiency. A compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself says the only difference between the chain and system levels "is in the number of
functionally interacting muscle groups" (printed 105), so system-level claims should be
checked against the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more
rigorously established category.

**Example** — **Inference:** a leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level
(single knee joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level
(hip, knee, and ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block
trains at the kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against
an external opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be
assumed to fully transfer to that system-level skill. This example is not in the source.

maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves

the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed

conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the

monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — The authors define the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. Relative to the body, the strength field also consists of two
systems: the *external interaction* with the motor apparatus, and the *internal
interaction* with the motor apparatus. The two appear simultaneously and act somewhat
independently, but influence each other increasingly as sports proficiency improves; control
of the external interaction "is possible only through the internal kinesiological pattern"
(printed 107). (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component; the text itself only
says each component "must be considered when ... selecting the special strength-training
means" (printed 107) without naming which method targets which component. **Inference:** a
movement that depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) plausibly calls for
plyometric or reactive methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force
(component 1) plausibly calls for more conventional strength methods; this mapping is not
stated in the text. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active
quadriceps/glute drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy
stored during the countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being
redirected (component 4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak
amortization phase is likely under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused
(component 1) training emphasis would not fix. This example and interpretation are not in
the source.
