# The Force-Time Curve Changes a Specific Way With Long-Term Training, and the Pattern Differs by Movement Type

**What it is** — As sports proficiency grows, an athlete's force-time curve F(t) changes in
a consistent three-stage sequence (Fig 2.3, printed pp. 98-99): (1) initially a relatively
uniform increase in force with an insignificant decrease in duration; (2) then a significant
increase in maximum force with a noticeable decrease in duration; (3) finally an increase in
the force developed at the beginning of the effort, with some further increase in maximum
and a decrease in the time taken to reach it. The overall pattern this leaves is: the time to
reach maximal force decreases, maximal force increases, the point of maximal effort moves
closer to the start of muscle tension, and the total duration of the effort decreases; the
same printed-100 summary also lists an increase in the working amplitude of the movement as
part of this general pattern (see the SSC sub-pattern below, which instead reports a
decrease). The authors report longitudinal data from one individual (Fig 2.2, a seated leg
task, before and after 6 months of strength training, captioned Siff & Verkhoshansky 1999)
and cite several other Soviet studies of athletes at different qualification levels as
corroborating support (PDF pp. 109-110, printed pp. 98-99, Figs 2.1-2.3). The authors then
describe four distinct sub-patterns by movement type, all sharing that same general trend
but differing in where force concentrates over the range of motion:
- **Large-resistance movements** (gymnastics, wrestling, weightlifting): perfecting is
  realised mainly by increasing maximum force with some decrease in time to produce it.
- **Ballistic/small-resistance movements** (fencing, some throwing): force concentrates near
  the *beginning* of the movement, shifting earlier and taking less time as mastery grows.
- **Stretch-shortening movements** (jumping, figure skating, acrobatics): perfecting comes
  from improving the muscles' ability to generate force during the eccentric-to-concentric
  transition, which *decreases* the working amplitude (a smaller joint-flexion angle) as
  mastery grows, the opposite direction from the general pattern's amplitude increase
  above; the text does not reconcile the two, and this entry does not either.
- **Cyclic movements** (running, swimming, rowing): perfecting comes from producing maximum
  force faster out of a deep, rapid relaxation phase, with a relatively longer relaxation
  phase and a shorter absolute cycle duration.
(PDF pp. 110-111, printed pp. 99-100, Figs 2.4-2.7.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no single unified mechanism for why the curve
reshapes this way across all four movement types; they attribute it to the general
perfecting of neuromuscular coordination and the kinesiological pattern (see
[[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]]) rather than a single
physiological cause. **Inference:** the movement-specific location of where force
concentrates is plausibly explained by task constraints (available time, external
resistance, and whether the movement uses a stretch-shortening cycle) shaping which part of
the range the nervous system learns to emphasize; no citation is offered for this and none
is added here.

**When to apply** — Use this as a framework for reading a force-time curve (e.g. a CMJ or
squat-jump trace from ForceDecks) against the athlete's event demands: a lineman's drive
block or a powerlifting-style movement should be read against the "large-resistance"
pattern (rising peak force, tightening time-to-peak), while a jump or plant-and-cut action
should be read against the "stretch-shortening" pattern (a shortening, more efficient
amortization). **Eric's baseline:** the department already runs the full ForceDecks CMJ
family and reports driver metrics like braking/propulsive force and phase durations under
the ODSF framework (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`, `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this framework
gives a training-adaptation lens for interpreting a trend in those phase-duration and
force metrics over a training block (e.g. a shortening amortization phase across a training
cycle) as a sign of the expected stretch-shortening-cycle adaptation, not just a data point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive pattern of *change over
training time*, not a same-day diagnostic; a single force-time trace cannot show whether an
athlete's curve is "improving" without a comparable baseline trace from earlier in that
athlete's training history. The four movement-type categories are the book's own taxonomy,
built from a handful of Soviet studies (Verkhoshansky 1961, 1963; Papysheva 1966; Gomberazde
1970; Semyenov 1970; Tatyan 1974) rather than a broad modern meta-analysis, so treat the
specific shapes (not just the general trend) as `supported`, not `proven`. Do not assume
every sport fits cleanly into one category; many football positions blend large-resistance
demands (line play) with stretch-shortening and cyclic demands (change of direction,
sprinting) within the same athlete.

**Example** — **Inference:** a running back's CMJ force-time trace, tracked across an
off-season block, would be expected (per this framework) to show a shortening, more
front-loaded braking phase and a higher, earlier propulsive peak as reactive strength
improves, distinct from an offensive lineman whose relevant curve (a drive-block or
isometric mid-thigh pull trace) would be expected to show a rising peak force with a
flatter, less time-compressed profile. Neither example is in the source.

**kinematic chain** (a sequential combination of several links working together, e.g. hip +
knee + ankle in a jump take-off), and the **kinematic system** (the combination of several
kinematic chains into one whole-body action, e.g. legs, torso, and shoulder girdle acting
together). Perfecting movement at each level has its own characteristic mechanism: at the
pair level, force output depends heavily on joint angle (maximum isometric force occurs at
a specific angle per joint, e.g. approximately 90 degrees for elbow flexion, 120 degrees for
elbow extension, 60-70 degrees for shoulder extension, 60 degrees for knee extension); at
the chain level, perfecting comes from increasing working amplitude, concentrating dynamic
force at a specific part of the range, and optimizing the sequencing of muscle
participation (proximal muscles initiate, distal links follow, with fixation at proximal
joints to create a stable base). Two resulting-force-less-than-sum examples the text flags
as not yet adequately analysed in the sporting literature (printed 103-104): (a) in
isolated elbow flexion, strength peaks isometrically near 90 degrees, but with simultaneous
shoulder extension and elbow flexion (stretching work), maximum isometric force shifts to
about 160 degrees at the elbow, and with propulsive work through the whole upper extremity,
maximal force develops with the elbow near full flexion, near the beginning of the push-off
(Campney & Wehr 1965); (b) with isolated knee extension, maximal force occurs in the
80-130 degree range, but with propulsive work through hip and knee together, maximal force
occurs near full hip extension and a knee angle close to 160 degrees (Dorofeyev 1965;
Yegorov 1966). At the system level, the same chain-level mechanisms extend across a larger
number of interacting muscle groups; "the only difference is in the number of functionally
interacting muscle groups," involving chiefly the strongest muscle groups of the legs and
torso, followed by the shoulder girdle. The process of perfecting movement from the
kinematic-pair level to the system level "is closely associated with the efficient
organisation and control of the motor action" (printed 105).

**Why it works** — The authors give a partial mechanism at the pair level: joint angle
changes muscle length and the angle of pull, which changes torque about the joint, which is
why force-angle curves are joint-specific (Figs 2.8-2.11, citing Zatsiorsky 1966;
Verkhoshansky 1970). At the chain level, they attribute the sequencing pattern to how the
body distributes work so that each joint operates near its own angle of maximum strength
where possible, with the deficit made up by stored elastic energy from a preceding
countermovement or amortization phase (e.g. the knee-extension assist from stored elastic
energy at the bottom of a vertical jump). **Inference:** no single unifying mechanism is
given for why analysis "levels" (pair vs. chain vs. system) should matter to a coach beyond
organizing the complexity of the problem; this is presented as a taxonomy for structuring
analysis, not itself a tested causal model.

**When to apply** — Use this taxonomy to decide what level of analysis (and therefore what
level of exercise) actually matches a sport skill: an isolated single-joint exercise trains
at the kinematic-pair level; Semyenov and Tatyanov (1976, printed 104) found a smaller
correlation between running and jumping performance and individual joint torques of the
lower extremity than between that performance and the force produced by the whole limb, a
correlation that strengthens further with proficiency. A compound lift like a
clean or a squat trains at the chain level; a sprint start or a blocking movement operates
at the whole-system level and cannot be fully represented by any single-joint or even
single-chain exercise. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection is already organized on a
general-to-specific spectrum (general preparation, specific preparation, specific
development, competitive exercises, per Bondarchuk) and weighted toward high
motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements with single-joint work kept to a small share
of volume (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13`, `week1-lecture.md p.31`). **Inference:** this
framework gives the underlying biomechanical reasoning for that weighting: whole-system,
chain-level exercises train the sequencing and joint-angle coordination that a sport skill
actually needs, while isolated single-joint work only trains the narrower kinematic-pair
level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive analysis taxonomy, not a
prescription that single-joint (kinematic-pair) work has no value; the book's own material
elsewhere treats isolated joint-angle training as informative for identifying weak links
(see [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). Do
not use "kinematic system" language as a stand-in for real coaching observation: the text
itself says the only difference between the chain and system levels "is in the number of
functionally interacting muscle groups" (printed 105), so system-level claims should be
checked against the same chain-level evidence rather than treated as a separate, more
rigorously established category.

**Example** — **Inference:** a leg-extension machine trains at the kinematic-pair level
(single knee joint, fixed angle range); a back squat trains at the kinematic-chain level
(hip, knee, and ankle sequenced together); a football offensive lineman's drive block
trains at the kinematic-system level (legs, torso, and arms coordinated as one unit against
an external opponent), and no amount of leg-extension or even squat work alone can be
assumed to fully transfer to that system-level skill. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]],
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1),
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]].

# Don't Infer Functional (Dynamic) Explosive Strength From an Isometric or Isokinetic Dynamometer

**What it is** — Standard textbook force-angle graphs are built from a dynamometer measuring
maximal isometric force at a series of fixed, successive joint angles, then fitting a curve
to those points; the authors report that Siff and mechanical-engineering students at the
University of the Witwatersrand, using high-speed video and tensiometers under
non-isokinetic dynamic conditions, confirmed Knapik et al (1983) in finding that the
resulting dynamic force-angle curves for a given joint differ significantly from the curves
obtained statically. The curve profile changes further with load, velocity of movement, and
joint orientation: for example, maximum torque for auxotonic (dynamic, variable-resistance)
elbow flexion does not occur near 90 degrees as isometric testing suggests, but nearer full
flexion, and evoking the myotatic stretch reflex with a ballistic start near full extension
produces yet another profile. The same divergence holds for isokinetic dynamometer curves
versus curves measured under unrestricted, free-weight or pulley conditions. Elsewhere in
the chapter, the authors state directly that isometric and isokinetic dynamometers "are
unable to measure functional maximal strength, Rate of Force Development or explosive
strength," so it is "futile" to use them to identify functional deficiencies bearing on
sporting preparedness or progress (PDF pp. 113-114, printed pp. 102-103; PDF p. 121, printed
p. 110; Figs 2.8-2.9, 2.14-2.15). This "futile" statement sits against the book's own
practice elsewhere: it computes explosive strength (Se) from isometric tension, "0.5 Fmax
over its time" (printed 102, 108); calls starting strength "always produced under
conditions of isometric muscle action" and says that fact "dispels the opinion that ...
isometric training should be completely abandoned" (printed 109); and builds the
functional/polyfunctional profile in part from "explosive-isometric muscular tension"
(printed 111-112, see
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]). The text
does not reconcile the "futile" statement with these uses; this entry does not resolve it
either.

**Why it works** — The authors' own stated reason, given for the force-angle curve
specifically, is that curves are "determined by the type of muscle contraction, the
velocity of movement, the starting conditions, the load and the orientation of the joint"
(printed 103). **Inference:** a broader mechanism (not stated in the text) is that
isometric and isokinetic devices fix either joint position or angular velocity, removing
the free acceleration, elastic-energy storage and release, and multi-joint coordination
that dynamic sporting movements actually use.

**When to apply** — Treat isometric and isokinetic dynamometer output (including a fixed-angle
isometric mid-thigh pull) as a specific, useful measure of force at that angle and condition,
not a general proxy for an athlete's dynamic explosive strength, sprint force application, or
jump performance. **Eric's baseline:** the isometric seated calf raise is run on the
ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting with a fixed 90-degree ankle/knee position
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`).
**Inference:** this caution argues for pairing that fixed-angle isometric data with a dynamic
measure (CMJ, sprint, or a dynamic strength test) rather than reporting the isometric number
alone as a proxy for an athlete's functional explosive capability; this specific pairing
recommendation is this entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: this entry sits against the book's own
internal contradiction described above (the "futile" statement versus the book's own
isometric-derived explosive-strength, starting-strength, and functional-profile measures),
and against vault evidence of a moderate real relationship. Thomas et al 2015 (vault,
`research-papers/thomas-2015-...`) found isometric mid-thigh pull (IMTP) impulse correlates
with countermovement-jump and squat-jump peak force and power (r = 0.49-0.64), though not
with jump height. **Inference:** this does not mean isometric or isokinetic testing has no
value; the text itself relies on isometric force-angle data throughout this chapter to
establish real, useful findings (e.g.
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]]), and notes isometric
testing "gives a fairly accurate picture of slow movement against very large resistance."
The caution is specifically against using these fixed-condition tests, alone, to infer
dynamic, functional, or explosive qualities, not against using them at all; the entry's
`contested` rating reflects that the book itself does not consistently follow its own
caution.

**Example** — An athlete's isometric mid-thigh pull peak force does not by itself tell you
whether that athlete produces force fast enough, in a free dynamic movement, to have a good
sprint start or CMJ; a high isometric peak measured at the wrong joint angle for the sport
skill can still coexist with poor dynamic explosive performance. The device itself cannot
measure rate of force development or explosive strength directly, per the authors' own
"futile" statement above, so a slow-RFD finding from an isometric test should not be cited
as evidence of that device's own output.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]],
[[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]],
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Chapter 1).

# The "Strength Field": Five Force Components That Make Up Every Sports Movement, and the "Kinesiological Pattern" That Organizes Them

**What it is** — The authors define the **strength field** of a motor task as the sum of
all external and internal forces acting on the body while it executes that task, made up of
five components: (1) the active driving force from muscular contraction, (2) the reactive
force arising from the active muscles' interaction with the environment, (3) force stored as
elastic energy in the muscle complex during a preparatory (stretching) phase, (4) the force
of inertia of the body or its links, and (5) the weight of the body or its links. The
**kinesiological pattern** is the specific, hierarchical organization of voluntary and
reflexive elements within that strength field for a given sport skill; he uses this term
rather than "biomechanical pattern" deliberately, to signal that a motor action is not just
physics acting on a body but an active process shaped by psychological and physiological
factors together. As sports mastery grows, the kinesiological pattern moves from weak,
irregularly distributed force elements (Fig 2.12a) to a tightly organized, hierarchical
system with dominant "key" elements and subordinate ones (Fig 2.12b), reproducible with less
variation and over a shorter time. Acyclic exercises (a single explosive effort) are trained
mainly by forming and refining this pattern; cyclic exercises (running, swimming) develop the
pattern faster and more simply, so training there centers more on perfecting involuntary,
repetitive contributions. Relative to the body, the strength field also consists of two
systems: the *external interaction* with the motor apparatus, and the *internal
interaction* with the motor apparatus. The two appear simultaneously and act somewhat
independently, but influence each other increasingly as sports proficiency improves; control
of the external interaction "is possible only through the internal kinesiological pattern"
(printed 107). (PDF pp. 116-118, printed pp. 105-107, sourced to Verkhoshansky
1958, 1963, 1966, 1968, 1977.)

**Why it works** — The author does not give a single causal mechanism for why the
kinesiological pattern tightens with mastery; he frames it as an emergent property of
repeated adaptation, where the correlation between elements strengthens (a change in one
element is reflected in others, even those separated in space and time) and a hierarchy of
dominant/subordinate elements forms. **Inference:** this is consistent with motor-learning
concepts of coordinative structure formation (movement components becoming functionally
linked with practice), though the text does not cite motor-learning literature directly to
support that link.

**When to apply** — Use the five-component strength field as a checklist when analyzing
why a movement produces the force output it does, and to decide which special-strength
training means (see later chapters) should target which component; the text itself only
says each component "must be considered when ... selecting the special strength-training
means" (printed 107) without naming which method targets which component. **Inference:** a
movement that depends heavily on stored elastic energy (component 3) plausibly calls for
plyometric or reactive methods, while one that depends mainly on the active driving force
(component 1) plausibly calls for more conventional strength methods; this mapping is not
stated in the text. **Inference:** this is a useful diagnostic lens for
reading a force-plate trace or coaching cue: ask which of the five components is limiting a
given athlete's output in a given task, rather than defaulting to "get stronger" as the only
lever.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this framework is a conceptual organizing scheme, not
a measured or validated model; the text gives no method for quantifying each of the five
components separately in a real sports movement, so treat it as a way to structure thinking
about a movement's force sources, not as a set of directly testable variables. Do not confuse
"kinesiological pattern" with a simple biomechanical description of joint angles over time;
the term is explicitly meant to include the reflexive and adaptive character of the pattern,
which a purely kinematic (position/angle) analysis would miss.

**Example** — **Inference:** in a vertical jump, the strength field includes the active
quadriceps/glute drive (component 1), ground reaction force (component 2), elastic energy
stored during the countermovement dip (component 3), the inertia of the body's mass being
redirected (component 4), and body weight (component 5); an athlete with a weak
amortization phase is likely under-using component 3, which a purely strength-focused
(component 1) training emphasis would not fix. This example and interpretation are not in
the source.

**Related** — [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]],
[[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Chapter 1),
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] (Chapter 1).

# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — The authors illustrate with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the curve comparison itself: athlete
A produces more force than B at any instant before crossover time T2 (a faster Rate of
Force Development), while B produces greater maximal force and sustains it longer. **Inference:**
maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities because most sporting
actions occur inside a limited time window; matching training to which of these two
qualities the sport actually uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say,
1RM strength) that the sport's time constraints never let the athlete express (see
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1).

**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
work. Eric's baseline also lists RFD among the "fluffy" metrics the ODSF framework adds
only "with a specific, defensible rationale" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); this principle is one such
rationale, not a baseline position on its own.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
eliminate either quality from a program.

**Example** — **Inference:** a cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break,
closing speed) are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value
from explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once
a baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.
This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--force-time-curve-adaptation-pattern-by-movement-type]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]] (Chapter 1).

# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups

**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and their own data, the authors describe building a
**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
running 12.1s versus 12.4s), the authors extend this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group on top of the raw strength topography: specifically, the
ratio of maximal strength to the time of its display "for explosive-isometric muscular
tension" (printed 111). This sits against the authors' own printed-110 statement (see
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]) that
isometric and isokinetic dynamometers cannot be used to identify functional deficiencies;
here the functional profile's speed index is itself built from isometric data. The text
does not reconcile this. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs 2.16-2.18.)

**Why it works** — The authors do not state why this profiling approach works beyond
observing that athletes with matched strength topography can still differ in performance
(the 12.1s vs. 12.4s sprinters). **Inference:** a profile organized by muscle group and
quality (strength peak, and separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific
groups are underdeveloped relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single
whole-body strength number cannot show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures
why two athletes with equal peak strength can still differ in performance, since the sport
may reward how fast that strength is expressed more than its ceiling (see
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).

**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real
usability problem, with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data dictionaries listed as
priority unfinished work (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`). **Inference:** this framework is
a direct conceptual match for that stated gap: a sport-specific dynamometric/functional
profile (per position group, not just per vendor) is essentially what the Development Plan's
proposed sport-specific data dictionary would need to support if it is to identify individual
athletes' weak links rather than just report raw device output; this specific mapping is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** building a useful general profile for a sport requires
a reasonably sized sample of athletes at that sport and level to establish what topography is
typical, which most single-team programs (including a college football roster split across
many position groups) will struggle to establish rigorously; a "general profile" built from a
handful of athletes risks reflecting individual variation rather than a real sport-typical
pattern. This is also a resource-intensive, multi-muscle-group testing approach; **Eric's
baseline** elsewhere states inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data and that
data collection has to be judged on cost versus insight (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy
and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`,
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); a full multi-joint dynamometric battery would need to
clear that same cost-versus-insight bar before being added to an already-running testing
menu.

**Example** — **Inference:** two running backs with equal 1RM back squats and equal CMJ
height could still differ in acceleration if one shows a slower rate of force development
specifically at hip extension; a functional profile built from isometric or force-plate
testing at each major joint action would surface that difference, where a single squat-max
or jump-height number would not. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]],
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]],
[[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]] (Chapter 1).

# A Sprinter's Absolute Leg Strength Has No Direct Correlation With Running Speed, but Connects to It Indirectly Through Jump Performance

**What it is** — The authors state there is no significant direct connection between
running speed and a sprinter's absolute leg strength, and that this connection is in fact
negative at the partial-correlation level (i.e., once other factors are controlled for, more
absolute leg strength is associated with less speed). However, there is a real, close
connection between absolute leg strength and jumping-exercise performance, and jumping
performance is in turn closely connected to running speed, so leg strength connects to sprint
speed indirectly through jump ability (Fig 2.23b). They extend the chain further with a
worked example: there is no direct significant connection between vertical jump height (h)
and absolute leg strength (So), but absolute strength determines the maximal force of the
take-off (Fmax), which determines the impulse of the push-off (F times t), which determines
jump height (PDF p. 129, printed p. 118). This sits against the authors' own statement two
sections later, in 3.3.3: "maximum strength is the main factor determining speed of
movement" (printed 151), where they pose this as a paradox in its own right: "why [do]
experiments show no correlation between absolute strength and speed of movement, whereas
under natural training conditions with an increase in strength, there is a corresponding
increase in speed" (printed 150-151), and say the answer is not yet settled. Both statements
are recorded here as given; the text does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the authors give the mechanical chain explicitly for the
jump example (absolute strength to maximal takeoff force to impulse to jump height) but does
not spell out why sprint speed itself fails to connect *directly* to leg strength; a plausible
reading, consistent with
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Chapter 1), is that sprinting at speed
uses leg strength at very different joint angles, contraction velocities, and ground-contact
times than a strength test measures, so raw strength predicts the shared underlying capacity
(impulse production) better than it predicts the sport skill (running speed) directly.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against expecting a simple squat-max-to-sprint-time
correlation, and instead track a mediating measure (jump height, jump-derived impulse or
power) as the more direct bridge between weight-room strength gains and sprint performance.
**Eric's baseline:** the Baylor Sport Assessment Table already pairs strength and jump/sprint
measures within the same sport-specific battery (CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower
strength estimation, linear sprint), rather than testing strength or speed alone
(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). **Inference:** this claim supports reading
jump metrics specifically as the connective tissue between a strength-training block's
results and expected sprint carryover, and argues against treating a stalled 40-yard-dash
time as evidence that more strength work is needed if jump metrics (the more directly
connected quality) haven't moved either.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested**: the authors themselves call maximum strength
"the main factor determining speed of movement" elsewhere in this same book (printed
150-151) and name the contradiction with this section's correlational finding as an
unresolved paradox. This is a single-lab, Soviet-era correlational finding (Verkhoshansky,
1977), not a controlled intervention study, and does not establish that increasing absolute
strength has no *causal* value for sprint speed, only that the two are not directly,
statistically connected in the samples studied. Do not use it to justify dropping strength
training for speed-dependent athletes; the mediating chain (strength to jump to speed) still
requires the strength link to function, and the book's own 3.3.3 material argues strength

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The authors (Verkhoshansky 1977) model an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. Specific abilities are described as, "in general, largely an
innate property of the motor apparatus," and developed "only by a particular motor regime"
(printed 121); more broadly, specific motor abilities "are more conservative" than the
structure of physical fitness as a whole, and their neuromuscular structure "is developed
only by a narrow range of means" (printed 122). (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122,
Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the authors do not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces. The book's own levelling
example is the decathlon 400m: as the negative correlation between the 100m and 1500m grows
more apparent with mastery, improvement in the 400m levels this out, decreasing the
100m-1500m connection while increasing the 100m-400m connection (printed 118-119, see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]). **Inference:** a football
equivalent might be a conditioning element that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from
degrading speed quality, but this application is not in the source.
**Inference:** this model maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

# Whether a Sport Rewards Fast Force (RFD) or Total Force/Momentum Should Decide Whether You Train Max Strength or Explosive Strength

**What it is** — The authors illustrate with a thought experiment (Fig 2.14-2.15): two
athletes perform a maximal single repetition of the same exercise as fast as possible, then
hold the load until fatigue. Athlete B produces a greater maximum force and sustains force
longer overall (greater area under the curve, i.e. greater momentum and muscle endurance).
Athlete A, however, produces *more* force than B at any early instant before a crossover time
T2 (i.e. a faster Rate of Force Development). If the sport requires rapid RFD (jumping,
striking, throwing sports such as basketball, martial arts, track and field), athlete A has
the advantage, and training aimed at increasing athlete B's maximal strength or muscle bulk
would be "misdirected" for that goal; that athlete instead needs explosive-strength (RFD)
training. If the sport instead requires high maximal force or momentum regardless of timing
(wrestling, powerlifting, rugby scrumming, judo), athlete B has the advantage, and athlete A
will not improve without training to increase maximal strength. (PDF pp. 120-121, printed pp.
109-110.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the curve comparison itself: athlete
A produces more force than B at any instant before crossover time T2 (a faster Rate of
Force Development), while B produces greater maximal force and sustains it longer. **Inference:**
maximal force and Rate of Force Development are separable qualities because most sporting
actions occur inside a limited time window; matching training to which of these two
qualities the sport actually uses avoids spending training time raising a quality (say,
1RM strength) that the sport's time constraints never let the athlete express (see
[[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], Chapter 1).

**When to apply** — Use this as a first screening question when assigning a training
emphasis: does this athlete's sport-critical action reward reaching a given force level fast
(most acyclic, ballistic, and reactive football actions: block shed, first-step acceleration,
change of direction) or reward sustained/maximal force output regardless of speed
(sustained drive-block engagement, some wrestling-style contact)? **Eric's baseline:** force
plate reporting already separates driver metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force) from
strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations) under the ODSF framework rather than reporting a
single peak-force number (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`). **Inference:** this principle supports reading those driver and
strategy metrics specifically for RFD-type signal (how fast, not just how much) when deciding
whether an athlete's programming should lean toward explosive-strength or maximal-strength
work. Eric's baseline also lists RFD among the "fluffy" metrics the ODSF framework adds
only "with a specific, defensible rationale" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`); this principle is one such
rationale, not a baseline position on its own.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a two-athlete illustration, not a controlled
study, and most football positions and actions are not purely RFD-limited or purely
force/momentum-limited; a single football play often requires both (e.g. an offensive lineman
needs fast initial force application off the snap AND sustained drive force through the
block). Do not use this principle to justify training only one quality at the expense of the
other for a position that plainly needs both; use it to set relative emphasis, not to
eliminate either quality from a program.

**Example** — **Inference:** a cornerback whose sport-critical actions (backpedal-to-break,
closing speed) are almost entirely time-limited would, per this principle, get more value
from explosive-strength/RFD-focused training than from chasing a higher back squat 1RM once
a baseline strength level is established; a nose tackle whose job includes anchoring against
sustained double-team drive would get more value from continuing to raise maximal strength.

# Map an Athlete's Strength "Topography" (Dynamometric/Functional Profile) to Find Underdeveloped Muscle Groups

**What it is** — Citing Uflyand (1965) and their own data, the authors describe building a
**dynamometric profile**: a visual map of the maximal strength of a representative set of
muscle groups for a given athlete (Fig 2.16 shows this for high jump versus distance running,
across trunk extension/flexion, thigh extension, ankle plantar/dorsiflexion). A **general
dynamometric profile**, built across many athletes of one specialization, characterizes the
strength topography typical of that sport and is preserved as sports mastery increases within
that group (Semyenov et al, 1971), though the exact rate of development for individual muscle
groups still varies. Because athletes with near-identical dynamometric profiles can still
produce very different competitive results (e.g. two sprinters with equal relative strength
running 12.1s versus 12.4s), the authors extend this to a **functional profile**
(sometimes called a "polyfunctional profile"), which adds the sport-relevant *speed*
qualities of each muscle group on top of the raw strength topography: specifically, the
ratio of maximal strength to the time of its display "for explosive-isometric muscular
tension" (printed 111). This sits against the authors' own printed-110 statement (see
[[heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-misrepresents-dynamic-functional-strength]]) that
isometric and isokinetic dynamometers cannot be used to identify functional deficiencies;
here the functional profile's speed index is itself built from isometric data. The text
does not reconcile this. (PDF pp. 121-123, printed pp. 110-112, Figs 2.16-2.18.)

**Why it works** — The authors do not state why this profiling approach works beyond
observing that athletes with matched strength topography can still differ in performance
(the 12.1s vs. 12.4s sprinters). **Inference:** a profile organized by muscle group and
quality (strength peak, and separately, speed of force development) exposes which specific
groups are underdeveloped relative to a sport's typical topography, which a single
whole-body strength number cannot show; adding the speed-of-development dimension captures
why two athletes with equal peak strength can still differ in performance, since the sport
may reward how fast that strength is expressed more than its ceiling (see
[[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]]).

**When to apply** — Use a per-muscle-group strength and RFD profile, benchmarked against
data from the athlete's own sport/position when available, to identify specific weak links
to target in programming, rather than programming purely off a general strength test.
**Eric's baseline:** the current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch,
ForceDecks, Polar) rather than by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis names as a real
usability problem, with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data dictionaries listed as
priority unfinished work (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`). **Inference:** this framework is
a direct conceptual match for that stated gap: a sport-specific dynamometric/functional
profile (per position group, not just per vendor) is essentially what the Development Plan's
proposed sport-specific data dictionary would need to support if it is to identify individual
athletes' weak links rather than just report raw device output; this specific mapping is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** building a useful general profile for a sport requires
a reasonably sized sample of athletes at that sport and level to establish what topography is
typical, which most single-team programs (including a college football roster split across

handful of athletes risks reflecting individual variation rather than a real sport-typical
pattern. This is also a resource-intensive, multi-muscle-group testing approach; **Eric's

# The Structure of Physical Fitness: Key, Specific, Non-Specific, and Levelling Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The authors (Verkhoshansky 1977) model an athlete's physical fitness as a hierarchy of
four kinds of motor ability (Fig 2.25): the **key motor ability (KMA)**, the integrated
ability that most directly determines competitive success in a given sport action, produced
by the combined development of a **specific ability (SA)** (which directly serves the key
ability's productivity) and a **non-specific ability (NSA)** (which does not itself satisfy
the sport's specific motor demand but assists when the specific ability alone is not enough,
e.g. muscular strength assisting speed of movement when external resistance is high); and
**levelling motor abilities (LMA)**, which smooth out negative correlations between the
specific and non-specific abilities, improve the connection between them, and expand the
functional range and adaptability of the key ability. Each of the specific and non-specific
abilities is itself built from a set of more basic **elementary abilities (EA)**, which stay
functionally independent and do not get "absorbed" into the key ability, but are integrated
by a **specific motor programme (SMP)** into a **specific neuromuscular structure (SNS)**
unique to that skill (worked example for explosive strength in Fig 2.26: the SMP integrates
starting-strength, absolute strength, acceleration-strength, and reactive ability into one
functional SNS). A non-specific ability can also actively hurt the key ability: the text gives
excessive absolute-strength development as an example of a non-specific ability that can
negatively affect speed. Specific abilities are described as, "in general, largely an
innate property of the motor apparatus," and developed "only by a particular motor regime"
(printed 121); more broadly, specific motor abilities "are more conservative" than the
structure of physical fitness as a whole, and their neuromuscular structure "is developed
only by a narrow range of means" (printed 122). (PDF pp. 131-133, printed pp. 120-122,
Figs 2.25-2.26.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the authors do not explain the neurophysiological basis
of the SMP/SNS integration process beyond naming it; the practical logic of the model is that
sporting success rarely depends on one isolated quality, and treating "the key ability" as a
single trainable target misses that it is actually assembled from at least two different
ability types (specific and non-specific) plus a smoothing/levelling function, each of which
may need distinct types of training exposure.

**When to apply** — Use this model when auditing a training program's coverage: for a given
sport-critical key ability, identify (1) what directly-specific quality is being trained, (2)
what non-specific "helper" quality is also feeding it and whether it's being trained
appropriately (not over- or under-emphasized), and (3) whether any levelling work exists to
resolve conflicts between the specific and non-specific pieces. The book's own levelling
example is the decathlon 400m: as the negative correlation between the 100m and 1500m grows
more apparent with mastery, improvement in the 400m levels this out, decreasing the
100m-1500m connection while increasing the 100m-400m connection (printed 118-119, see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]). **Inference:** a football
equivalent might be a conditioning element that keeps a heavy-strength emphasis from
degrading speed quality, but this application is not in the source.
**Inference:** this model maps onto Eric's baseline's stated training-compatibility constraint that
incompatible qualities are not trained at full intensity in the same block, and that
compatible qualities are trained together while the rest are trained at a retention dose
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`); the levelling-ability concept here gives a
possible mechanism for why some quality combinations are compatible (a levelling ability
smooths their interaction) and others are not, though this specific mechanistic link is this
entry's own reading, not stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual model, not a measured or directly
testable one; the text gives no protocol for identifying which of an athlete's abilities are
"key" versus "non-specific" versus "levelling" in a given sport beyond correlational and
factor-analytic study of large athlete samples (see
[[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]]), which most single-team programs
cannot replicate. Do not use this model to justify adding more distinct "levelling"
exercises without evidence that a specific conflict between two trained qualities actually
exists; the model describes an interaction that can occur, not one that always needs a
dedicated training solution.

**Example** — **Inference:** for a defensive lineman, the key motor ability might be a fast
first movement off the ball. The specific ability feeding it could be starting-strength/RFD
work; a non-specific ability assisting it could be absolute strength (helps when facing a
heavier blocker); but if heavy absolute-strength training starts to slow the athlete's first
movement (the negative-influence case the text does name, for speed generally), some
levelling element (e.g. continued speed-strength or reactive work alongside the strength
block) would be needed to keep the non-specific quality from degrading the key ability. This
football application is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--motor-ability-connection-types-taxonomy]],
[[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]],
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] (Chapter 1).

---
chapter: "3.1"

# Eccentric Actions Produce More Force and Cost Less Energy Than Concentric, by Specific Cited Margins

**What it is** — Three related, separately-sourced findings on eccentric versus concentric
muscular work: (1) **Force**: a maximal overcoming (concentric) contraction produces
1.2-1.6x less force than the same muscle displays resisting a stretch (eccentric), per
Bethe (1929); cited examples of eccentric-over-concentric superiority are 22% for the
arms, 46.8% for the forearms, and 50% for the knee extensors. Semyonov's 1968 data on
untrained subjects gives maximal isometric knee-extensor force at 120° as 465 N versus 401
N concentric; combined-regime testing found the largest force (50? N, the last digit
unclear at the page edge/image resolution, PDF p. 137, printed p. 126, so cannot be
confirmed as exactly 506) for slow eccentric action following preliminary maximal isometric
tension, and 453 N for eccentric following preliminary concentric work. (2) **Energy
cost**: eccentric work uses roughly half the energy of concentric work, but this advantage
is displayed only with slow movements *and large loads* (Chauveau, 1904; corroborated by
later work: Fenn 1924, Hartree & Hill 1928, Hill 1930, Cattel 1983); the text explicitly
states there is no reason to associate this advantage with the potential for quick,
powerful concentric-style movements.
(3) **Reflex mechanism**: the myotatic stretch reflex strengthens with the speed of the
stretch (Samoyloff & Kisseleff 1928; Foerster & Altenburg 1933; Lippold 1957), and better-trained
athletes use this reflex tension more precisely and efficiently during eccentric work
(Zakharyents, 1962). (PDF pp. 136-137, printed pp. 125-126, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work.")

**Why it works** — The authors state that the myotatic stretch reflex "has great
significance for increasing the working effect of eccentric work," and that its strength
scales with the speed of the stretch; they give no mechanism for why a well-trained
athlete's reflex use is more precise and efficient, and no mechanism for Bethe's
force ratio itself. For (2), the text does not give a mechanistic explanation beyond citing
the calorimetric/heat studies. **Inference:** a plausible explanation, not stated anywhere
in the book, is that fewer cross-bridges cycle per unit of force produced during slow
forcible lengthening than during shortening; this is offered here only as a plausible guess,
not a cited finding.

**When to apply** — Useful as a citable, quantified starting point for programming
eccentric-emphasis work (e.g. eccentric overload machines, tempo-eccentric lifting,
eccentric hamstring work) where the goal is either a large force stimulus at relatively
low metabolic/cardiovascular cost, or building the reflex-tension precision the text
associates with trained athletes. **Eric's baseline:** the corpus documents NordBord
eccentric hamstring testing, retained for targeted return-to-play groups paired with
joint-specific isometric testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`), but no eccentric-emphasis
*training* protocol is documented, so this is a gap this text could inform if the department
wants a citable rationale for adding eccentric-emphasis training blocks.

**When NOT to apply** — All three numbers sets are single old studies (1929, 1968, 1904,
with corroborating work through 1983), largely on isolated joints or untrained subjects,
not independently re-validated within this ingest; treat the specific percentages (22%,
46.8%, 50%, the halved-energy figure) as illustrative orders of magnitude from that era's
methods, not as targets to program against directly. The energy-saving finding explicitly
does not apply above 0.12 m/s, so it cannot be used to justify eccentric training as
"more efficient" for fast, powerful, sport-relevant velocities.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "eccentric strength exceeds concentric by up to
50%" for knee extensors should note that the text does not name a citation for the 22%,
46.8%, or 50% figures specifically; Semyonov's (1968) cited data instead compare isometric
force (465 N) with concentric force (401 N), not eccentric with concentric. Treat all these
figures as single-era estimates for that joint, not universal strength-training constants.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (the elastic-energy
storage mechanism eccentric loading exploits); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(the same stretch-speed-dependent reflex potentiation, applied to plyometric training).

---
chapter: "3.1"

# Eight Types of Muscular Tension, Classified by How and How Fast Force Is Displayed

**What it is** — Beyond the basic mechanical regimes (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic,
isokinetic, quasi-isometric; already covered in Ch1, see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]), Siff and Verkhoshansky classify the
*character* of muscular tension in sport into at least eight types, organized by how
quickly tension develops, its magnitude, duration, repetitions, and the muscle's
pre-working state. The authors call this eight-type split "central to the subsequent
discussion of special strength training in sport" (printed 127): **tonic** (large,
prolonged tension where speed of development doesn't matter much, e.g. holding a pin in
wrestling or a barbell overhead; tonic tension can also be of a much smaller magnitude when
holding a pose, e.g. in pistol shooting or gymnastics); **phasic** (cyclic,
rhythmic tension-relaxation, e.g. rowing, swimming, cycling, distance running); **phasic-tonic**
(switching between dynamic and stabilizing work within one skill, e.g. gymnastics,
judo, wrestling); **explosive-isometric** (large resistance overcome, force maximum reached
isometrically at the end of the movement, e.g. snatching or jerking a barbell, and the
brief eccentric-to-concentric transition in plyometrics); **explosive-ballistic** (small
relative resistance, force peaks early/mid-movement then the load coasts on inertia, e.g.
shotput, javelin, tennis serve); **explosive-reactive-ballistic** (same as ballistic but with
a sharp, pronounced preliminary stretch immediately before the concentric phase, e.g. some
throws, wrestling and volleyball actions); and two **speed types**: acyclic (a single quick
momentary contraction, e.g. a boxing punch) and cyclic (repeated actions at a fast tempo
where each cycle's working effect must be sustained, e.g. sprinting). (PDF pp. 136-140,
printed pp. 125-129, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work," Fig 3.1; the authors credit the whole
of Fig 3.1, not just the eight-type split, as their own convenience classification, not an
exhaustive or definitive taxonomy: "we do not pretend to have classified all the forms.")

**Why it works** — The authors argue this classification exists because a "universal
regime of muscular work to develop strength" doesn't exist: which regime dominates a
given sport skill depends jointly on the magnitude, duration, and speed of tension
required, so training method selection has to be matched to the specific tension-type a
skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy: several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one
category can be as misleading as ignoring the distinction altogether. Do not use this as a
testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — **Inference:** a boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure
quickness) versus a heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back
(explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look
superficially similar but sit in different cells of this classification, implying different
primary training levers (reaction/movement time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style
work for the power punch). This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (the underlying mechanical
regimes this classification builds on); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(explosive-isometric tension's plyometric transition phase); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the force-time analysis that follows for explosive-type tensions).

chapter: "3.2.1"

# Reaction Latency Is Largely Fixed; Decision Time and Movement Time Are Trainable

**What it is** — "Quickness" (rapid CNS-driven muscle contraction/relaxation without
preliminary stretch, against negligible resistance) is measured as **reaction time**
(stimulus to response/movement-initiation) and is distinct from **movement time** (end of
the reaction phase to end of the movement); the text states no correlation has been
demonstrated between the two (Harbin et al, 1989). Average simple reaction times by
modality: 0.142 s auditory, 0.155 s tactile, 0.194 s visual (Harbin et al, 1989); fully
unpredictable visual signals push reaction time above 0.5 s (Fogel, 1963). Reaction time
splits into a latency phase (stimulus to first EMG activity) and a response phase (EMG
onset to motor action); Hanes & Schall (1996) attribute reaction-time variability to how
fast a monkey's neuronal firing rate reaches a fixed movement-triggering threshold, not to
nerve conduction velocity differences. The text states the **latency period is determined
largely by genetics and minimally affected by training**, so quickness improvement has to
come from the movement/response phase: the average simple unidirectional movement time
(0.3 s) can decrease by more than 50% in highly trained subjects. For complex tasks
requiring anticipation/decision-making (e.g. striking or catching a fast-moving object),
performance depends more on accurately anticipating trajectory than on raw reaction speed
alone. The text states directly that "enhanced strength is of little value if the athlete
does not maintain or improve neuromuscular ability" (printed 134), and that reaction time
"comprises a sensing time and a decision time, with the latter in particular improving
through the regular application of neuromuscular skill training" (printed 134); "movement
time is strongly influenced by motor coordination or precision of movement" (printed 135).
Elsewhere in the same section (printed 140), the text states that "quickness is a general
quality of the CNS ... determined by genetic factors, and therefore the potential for its
development is limited," while separately, "speed of movement ... [has] far greater
potential to enhance" than quickness does; this entry records both the latency-is-fixed
finding here and that later statement rather than picking one. (PDF pp. 144-146, printed
pp. 133-135, "Quickness and Reactive Ability"; PDF p. 151, printed p. 140.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that latency reflects largely fixed
neural-transmission and central-processing constraints: peripheral sensory-to-CNS and

# Eight Types of Muscular Tension, Classified by How and How Fast Force Is Displayed

**What it is** — Beyond the basic mechanical regimes (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic,
isokinetic, quasi-isometric; already covered in Ch1, see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]), Siff and Verkhoshansky classify the
*character* of muscular tension in sport into at least eight types, organized by how
quickly tension develops, its magnitude, duration, repetitions, and the muscle's
pre-working state. The authors call this eight-type split "central to the subsequent
discussion of special strength training in sport" (printed 127): **tonic** (large,
prolonged tension where speed of development doesn't matter much, e.g. holding a pin in
wrestling or a barbell overhead; tonic tension can also be of a much smaller magnitude when
holding a pose, e.g. in pistol shooting or gymnastics); **phasic** (cyclic,
rhythmic tension-relaxation, e.g. rowing, swimming, cycling, distance running); **phasic-tonic**
(switching between dynamic and stabilizing work within one skill, e.g. gymnastics,
judo, wrestling); **explosive-isometric** (large resistance overcome, force maximum reached
isometrically at the end of the movement, e.g. snatching or jerking a barbell, and the
brief eccentric-to-concentric transition in plyometrics); **explosive-ballistic** (small
relative resistance, force peaks early/mid-movement then the load coasts on inertia, e.g.
shotput, javelin, tennis serve); **explosive-reactive-ballistic** (same as ballistic but with
a sharp, pronounced preliminary stretch immediately before the concentric phase, e.g. some
throws, wrestling and volleyball actions); and two **speed types**: acyclic (a single quick
momentary contraction, e.g. a boxing punch) and cyclic (repeated actions at a fast tempo
where each cycle's working effect must be sustained, e.g. sprinting). (PDF pp. 136-140,
printed pp. 125-129, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work," Fig 3.1; the authors credit the whole
of Fig 3.1, not just the eight-type split, as their own convenience classification, not an
exhaustive or definitive taxonomy: "we do not pretend to have classified all the forms.")

**Why it works** — The authors argue this classification exists because a "universal
regime of muscular work to develop strength" doesn't exist: which regime dominates a
given sport skill depends jointly on the magnitude, duration, and speed of tension
required, so training method selection has to be matched to the specific tension-type a
skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy: several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one

testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — **Inference:** a boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure
quickness) versus a heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back
(explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look
superficially similar but sit in different cells of this classification, implying different
primary training levers (reaction/movement time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style
work for the power punch). This example is not in the source.

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" (the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax)) changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs

upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which

the growing deficit at lower resistance shown in the table.

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**, which the text defines three ways without fully reconciling
them: earlier (2.2.1, printed 108) as "the explosive strength index relative to body
weight," RC = Fmax/(tmax.W) = RFDmax/W; here, the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two
characteristics of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the
field-practical form **RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time
to reach it, m is the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Despite
that formula, the text separately states that in the reactivity test itself, "the
coefficient of reactivity was determined from the length of the support period and analysis
of the mean take-off force" (printed 137), not a literal Fmax/tmax calculation; the text
does not explain how the two are reconciled. Verkhoshansky's own "reactivity test" protocol:
a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after a depth-jump from 0.4 m,
unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added (fixed absolute loads, not expressed as a
percentage of the athlete's So); jump height and support-period duration are recorded and
plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** this
framework is a plausible historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g)
versus mRSI = jump height / time to take-off, not contact time); this lineage claim is not
stated in either source. The load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself: it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different
RC/RSI: Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or
improves) as external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one
whose reactive ability only shows up unloaded. The former likely has more absolute strength
to draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity. This example is not
in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the plyometric
training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).
=== claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations.md
---
chapter: "3.3.2"
