# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits

**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0): that is,
maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
stretch-related (SSC) processes: stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. The book itself does not offer a neural or other mechanism for why
the two curves diverge; a plausible modern reading is that the low-velocity plateau
reflects voluntary neural inhibition rather than a true mechanical property, but the
sources for that specific claim are not in this ingest's vault or the source text, so it is
not cited here (verify before adding). Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling
broadly: it is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions
specifically, not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off. Separately, the
book states plainly that "the Hill and Perrine-Edgerton curves do not apply to actions
which strongly recruit the stretch reflex or involve the release of stored elastic energy"
(printed 152), which further narrows where either curve should be trusted.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer
data near zero velocity should not be assumed to predict an athlete's true near-isometric
force output accurately, per the Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs
at a low, non-zero velocity rather than at V=0. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force: that is,
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg, roughly two-thirds of their maximum**,
producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at maximal load,
and time to execute the lift "increases by 282%" (the text does not state the reference
point this percentage is measured from). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The
Effect of the Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically. Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 (vault, `research-papers/jandacka-2008-...`) found
lower optimal countermovement-squat loads, about 47% ± 9% for men and 54% ± 9% for women,
and concluded no single percentage fits all lifters; **Inference:** treat this book's
65-70% figure as this specific 1970s powerlifting dataset's own finding, not a fixed
modern target. **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, both figures argue for
triangulating against the department's own velocity-based methods (Perch) rather than
applying either fixed percentage as a rule.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat), and
the book does not date the study; it should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic
lifts, ballistic movements, upper body pressing) without separate data, and it does not
override or replace the classical 25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint
contractions that figure was actually derived from: the two describe different kinds of
movement, not contradictory answers to the same question.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power
output at "25% of maximal isometric force" (the classical isotonic-model figure, not a 1RM
percentage) would badly undershoot the load that actually produces peak power output in the
real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).

---
chapter: "3.3.2"

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism for the three-zone shape itself. Earlier in
the same discussion, it gives gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system as
the reason single-joint, isolated-muscle studies transfer poorly to multi-jointed movement
generally, not specifically as the stated cause of the three zones. The practical takeaway
offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling. **Inference:** if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a
cyclic-sport athlete, this single 1985 study would predict a three-zone pattern rather than
a single smooth hyperbola; treat this as this entry's own extrapolation, not a source
recommendation to expect that pattern going forward.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]; the book does not
reconcile all three pictures. Modern whole-body sprint force-velocity profiling instead
finds a linear, decreasing relation, not a three-zone curve (Samozino et al 2016, vault,
`research-papers/samozino-2016-...`; Morin, vault, `research-papers/morin-undated-1-...`).
None of these pictures should be treated as the settled, final description of the human
force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to
a sprinter's treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not assume, without checking, that the
mid-velocity range shows force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading
off; modern sprint force-velocity profiling (Samozino 2016, vault) instead finds a linear
decreasing relation. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). This velocity-based framing sits
against how the same two terms were defined earlier in the book (2.2.1, printed 107-108):
there, explosive strength is "the ability to produce maximal force in a minimal time," with
no velocity band attached, and speed-strength is "the ability to quickly execute an
unloaded movement or a movement against a relatively small external resistance," which is a
load-based definition, not the "intermediate velocity" placement used here. The text does
not reconcile the two framings, and this entry does not either. The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision: it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline** already names "strength-speed/speed-strength
work" as a category athletes shift toward once already strong (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`); this
framework gives the definitions behind those two already-named terms, rather than adding a
new category the baseline lacks.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale: there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — **Inference:** a heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed
(strength-dominant power); a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength
(speed-dominant power). The book gives no %1RM load bands for either category; these
percentages are this entry's own illustration, not sourced. Both are "explosive" in casual
language, but this framework says they train different ends of the same continuum and
should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy, CFmax/TFmax/Fmm, not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force. **Inference:** RC's specific
formula (force over time-to-peak times system mass) is not explained sentence-by-sentence
in the text beyond this general stretch-energy mechanism; the fact that it tracks support-period
time more tightly than raw force output is reported as an empirical correlation finding,
not derived from a stated causal mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** this
framework is a plausible historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g)
versus mRSI = jump height / time to take-off, not contact time); this lineage claim is not
stated in either source. The load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself: it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different
RC/RSI: Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or
improves) as external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one
whose reactive ability only shows up unloaded. The former likely has more absolute strength
to draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity. This example is not
in the source.

training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).
=== claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations.md

# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits

**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0): that is,
maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
stretch-related (SSC) processes: stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. The book itself does not offer a neural or other mechanism for why
the two curves diverge; a plausible modern reading is that the low-velocity plateau
reflects voluntary neural inhibition rather than a true mechanical property, but the
sources for that specific claim are not in this ingest's vault or the source text, so it is
not cited here (verify before adding). Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling
broadly: it is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions
specifically, not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off. Separately, the
book states plainly that "the Hill and Perrine-Edgerton curves do not apply to actions
which strongly recruit the stretch reflex or involve the release of stored elastic energy"
(printed 152), which further narrows where either curve should be trusted.

**Example** — **Inference:** a force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer
data near zero velocity should not be assumed to predict an athlete's true near-isometric
force output accurately, per the Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs
at a low, non-zero velocity rather than at V=0. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force: that is,
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg, roughly two-thirds of their maximum**,
producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at maximal load,
and time to execute the lift "increases by 282%" (the text does not state the reference
point this percentage is measured from). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The
Effect of the Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism beyond noting the mismatch between
idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a multi-joint,
whole-body competition lift. **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits many muscle
groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties, technique
constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot capture,
which could explain why the practical power-peak load sits well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction, but the book itself does not offer this or any other explanation.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically. Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 (vault, `research-papers/jandacka-2008-...`) found
lower optimal countermovement-squat loads, about 47% ± 9% for men and 54% ± 9% for women,
and concluded no single percentage fits all lifters; **Inference:** treat this book's
65-70% figure as this specific 1970s powerlifting dataset's own finding, not a fixed
modern target. **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, both figures argue for
triangulating against the department's own velocity-based methods (Perch) rather than
applying either fixed percentage as a rule.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat), and
the book does not date the study; it should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic
lifts, ballistic movements, upper body pressing) without separate data, and it does not
override or replace the classical 25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint
contractions that figure was actually derived from: the two describe different kinds of
movement, not contradictory answers to the same question.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power
output at "25% of maximal isometric force" (the classical isotonic-model figure, not a 1RM
percentage) would badly undershoot the load that actually produces peak power output in the
real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).
=== claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion.md

chapter: "3.3.2"

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — The text gives no mechanism for the three-zone shape itself. Earlier in
the same discussion, it gives gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system as
the reason single-joint, isolated-muscle studies transfer poorly to multi-jointed movement
generally, not specifically as the stated cause of the three zones. The practical takeaway
offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling. **Inference:** if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a
cyclic-sport athlete, this single 1985 study would predict a three-zone pattern rather than
a single smooth hyperbola; treat this as this entry's own extrapolation, not a source
recommendation to expect that pattern going forward.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]; the book does not
reconcile all three pictures. Modern whole-body sprint force-velocity profiling instead
finds a linear, decreasing relation, not a three-zone curve (Samozino et al 2016, vault,
`research-papers/samozino-2016-...`; Morin, vault, `research-papers/morin-undated-1-...`).
None of these pictures should be treated as the settled, final description of the human
force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to
a sprinter's treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not assume, without checking, that the
mid-velocity range shows force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading
off; modern sprint force-velocity profiling (Samozino 2016, vault) instead finds a linear
decreasing relation. This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).
=== framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones.md

chapter: "3.3.3"

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). This velocity-based framing sits
against how the same two terms were defined earlier in the book (2.2.1, printed 107-108):
there, explosive strength is "the ability to produce maximal force in a minimal time," with
no velocity band attached, and speed-strength is "the ability to quickly execute an
unloaded movement or a movement against a relatively small external resistance," which is a
load-based definition, not the "intermediate velocity" placement used here. The text does
not reconcile the two framings, and this entry does not either. The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision: it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline** already names "strength-speed/speed-strength
work" as a category athletes shift toward once already strong (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`); this
framework gives the definitions behind those two already-named terms, rather than adding a
new category the baseline lacks.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale: there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — **Inference:** a heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed
(strength-dominant power); a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength
(speed-dominant power). The book gives no %1RM load bands for either category; these
percentages are this entry's own illustration, not sourced. Both are "explosive" in casual
language, but this framework says they train different ends of the same continuum and
should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy, CFmax/TFmax/Fmm, not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

# Round-2 review: Supertraining Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 to 3.4.2 (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent round-2 pass), 2026-09-27. Read-only on entries and sources.
Round 1: `staging/review_supertraining_ch2-3a_opus.md` (0 GO, 35 FIX, 1 NO-GO, G1-G8). Fixer log: `staging/fixes_supertraining_ch2-3a_applied.md`.
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch2-3a.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`. All 36 exist.

## Status convention

- **FIXED**: every round-1 item for the row is resolved in the file, and nothing new of substance was introduced.
- **STILL FIX**: at least one round-1 item (row item or G1-G6) remains. If the fix also introduced a problem, it is listed in the same row.
- **NEW PROBLEM**: the round-1 items are resolved, but the fix introduced a new defect.

## How this was checked

- Every one of the 36 files was read in full (body text, not the fixer log).
- **Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer page = printed + 12):** 126 (printed 114, pole vault, Fig 2.21, heterochronicity order), 128 (printed 116, transfer and Krestovnikov paragraphs), 153 (printed 141, Table 3.2), 155-156 (printed 143-144, partial vs absolute endurance, carry-over, pre-working states), 165-167 (printed 153-155, 160 degree finding, pelvic tilt, head and eye position, asymmetry), 171-172 (printed 159-160, age section, Table 3.6, eqs 3.8-3.9, worked example), 176-177 (printed 164-165, after-effect, 90%, Ilin timing).
- **Text only (PyMuPDF extraction of PDF 104-179):** printed 108-109 (three strength-endurance forms), 118 (connection types), 131, 133 (factor structure, "very little or no effect"), 134-135 and 140 (reaction and quickness quotes), 145 (pre-working mechanism), 151 (strength-speed paradox), 157 (bodymass correlations), 162 (Gompertz, Siff and Medvedev), 125-126 (eccentric "slow movements and large loads").
- Mechanical checks over all 36 files: inline em dashes (0 outside section headers); review-history words; "(verify)"; unlabeled Examples; voice ("he", "the author", "Verkhoshansky states"); every `[[wikilink]]` resolved against the vault library and the staging library (all resolve); every `research-papers/...` reference.
- Vault papers opened to confirm the cited numbers: Jandacka 2008 (47 ± 9% men, 54 ± 9% women), Kozinc 2022 (48.4% of participants), Hirayama 2014 (+4.3%, +6.7%, +10.0%), Hanson 2007 (no clear enhancement), Thomas 2015. All match the entries.
- Vault search for the external papers round 1 marked "verify" (Dudley 1990, Westing 1990, Saraceni 2020, Blazevich and Babault 2019, any PAPE source): none are in the vault. The entries that dropped the names but kept the claims are flagged below (G-row "uncited modern claims").
- `docs/method-baseline.md` read for every "Eric's baseline:" line.

## Fixer log vs files (where the log overstates)

1. **G1.** Log: "Every Example not already labeled was prefixed Inference." Files: three Examples are still unlabeled inventions: `heuristic--isometric-dynamometry-...`, `claim--secular-increase-...-gompertz-growth`, `claim--pap-findings-contested-...`.
2. **G3.** Log: every flagged line "now cites the specific method-baseline.md section/source file". Files: posture, pelvic tilt and head position cite the Bondarchuk exercise-spectrum bullet (`class1 pp.13-16`, `week1 pp.32-36`) for "clean, snatch, jerk, squat" coaching. The baseline names only "squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints" (Strength and power, the core/ballistic bullet, `class1 p.13`, `week1 p.31`); it never names the snatch, jerk or deadlift. Strength-deficit and strength-endurance still put an inference under the "Eric's baseline:" label.
3. **Vault links.** Log: "Added the three vault papers" and similar in six entries. Files: all 11 references are truncated paths such as `research-papers/thomas-2015-...`; none is a resolvable link. Full filenames are in the table at the end.
4. **Female-male ratio.** Log: "Moved the raw-JSON extraction process note out of the entry." File: the parenthetical is still there ("verified directly against the PDF page image, see `_book.md` process note on the text-extraction discrepancy"), and `_book.md` has no such note (grep for "extraction", "masticat", "0.80": no match).
5. **Pre-working state.** Log: "Replaced the invented mechanism with the text's actual stated reason (printed 145)." File: the printed-145 reason ("When the muscles are relaxed or in a state of isometric tension, the speed and power of their subsequent contraction is determined primarily by the nervous impulses to the muscles") is absent, and the entry now describes a "less time/force" gloss that no longer appears in it.
6. **Age entry.** Log: "Relabeled When to apply 'Inference:'." File: the first sentence of When to apply is unlabeled and is not the book's reasoning (see the full review below).

## 1. Full review: `claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations` (round 1 NO-GO)

Checked on the page images (viewer 171-172, printed 159-160):

- Correct now: peak "between the ages of about 20 and 28 years", "approximately 1% per annum" (printed 159); Hettinger et al 1961 and MacDougall et al 1982; Masters "over 40 years of age"; Table 3.6 age 10 lab 42 / lifting 59 and age 65 lab 74 / lifting 49; disagreement "younger than about 14 or those over 45 years"; the two explanations; "linear regression accurately describes the decrease of strength after the age of 30"; eq 3.8 `%S = 120.17 - 0.68865 A (R = 0.988)`, eq 3.9 `%S = 140.15 - 1.3853 A (R = 0.996)`, both "between 30 and 80 years"; the slope ratio (1.3853 / 0.68865 = 2.01); the worked example (A = 86.3%, B = 67.8%, %S at 45 = 77.8%, final B = 87.1%; 67.8 / 0.778 = 87.1). Locator PDF 170-171, printed 159-160 is right. Direction of the disagreement is now correct, so the NO-GO is lifted.
- Remaining problems:
  1. **Line 60 is review history.** "This reasoning is rebuilt from the corrected direction of the lab-versus-lifting disagreement above; an earlier draft of this entry had that direction reversed." Replacement: delete both clauses (the whole When to apply paragraph is replaced in item 2).
  2. **When to apply, first sentence, is unlabeled and is not the book's reasoning.** "isolated dynamometer or force-plate testing may better isolate raw strength for very young or very old populations, while competition-style multi-joint lift performance folds in accumulated technical skill". The book never mentions force plates or technical skill here; its young-end reason is training status (trained children vs untrained peers), its old-end reason is agility and strength-speed across many muscle groups. The Baylor Inference that follows then argues from "technical proficiency", which is neither of the book's reasons.
  3. **Why it works, lines 45-48, contradicts the page.** "they present lab and lifting as two different measurements of different things, not one measurement that is closer to the truth than the other." The text calls the young lifters' scores "higher than expected" and the older lifters' "lower than expected" (printed 160), i.e. it takes the lab curve as the expectation.
  4. **Hedges dropped.** "which the text attributes to" (twice): the text says "probably due to" (children) and "possibly due to" (over 45).
  5. Minor: the title "Declines About 1% a Year After 30" merges the printed-159 "1% per annum" (from the 20-28 peak) with the regressions' 30-80 range, while the entry body correctly says neither equation gives 1%.
- Exact corrections:
  - What it is: replace "which the text attributes to weight-trained children being much stronger" with "which the text says is 'probably due to' weight-trained children being much stronger"; replace "which the text attributes to Olympic weightlifting's added demand" with "which the text says is 'possibly due to' Olympic weightlifting's added demand".
  - Why it works: replace lines 45-48 ("The authors do not frame this ... than the other.") with: "The text calls the prepubescent lifters' scores 'higher than expected' and the older lifters' scores 'lower than expected' (printed 160), so it treats the laboratory curve as the reference and gives each explanation as probable, not proven."
  - When to apply: replace the whole paragraph (lines 50-61) with:
    "**When to apply** — The authors' stated use of eqs 3.8-3.9 is to compare the relative strength of lifters of different ages, applied after the bodymass adjustment (printed 160; see Example). Do not treat laboratory and lifting percentages as interchangeable below about 14 or over about 45: lifting runs above lab in children (probably a training-status difference between the samples) and below lab over 45 (possibly the agility and strength-speed demands of weightlifting) (printed 160). **Inference:** Table 3.6 puts 18-year-olds at about 83-84% of peak and 20-year-olds at 93-97% (the two methods agree closely there), so part of a freshman-to-senior strength gain on a college roster may be maturation rather than training; the book gives no college-athlete data, so treat this as a caution when reading class-year strength changes, not as a correction factor."
  - Title (optional): "Strength Peaks at About 20-28 and Then Declines; Lab and Competition Data Disagree Below 14 and Over 45".
- Verdict now: **STILL FIX** (downgraded from NO-GO: the headline direction, threshold, equations and example are right; the remaining defects are one paragraph, one sentence and two hedges).
